item.title: F.B.I. Charges American in Plot Behind Canada’s Tumbler Ridge School Shooting
item.description:
The U.S. authorities arrested a 30-year-old Washington State resident on Tuesday on charges of conspiring to commit a school shooting in rural British Columbia, eight months after a Canadian teenager killed eight people.

On Feb. 10, Jesse Van Rootselaar, 18, shot and killed her mother and 11-year-old stepbrother in Tumbler Ridge, British Columbia, a tranquil mountain town. She then went to the local school and shot and killed five students and one educational instructor. She died in the school of a self-inflicted gunshot wound, and her death prompted the Royal Canadian Mounted Police to announce they were not searching for any other suspects.

But on Tuesday afternoon, officials from the Federal Bureau of Investigation, Royal Canadian Mounted Police and the U.S. Department of Justice announced that another person had, for months, been in contact with Ms. Van Rootselaar to plot the shooting. That included sending cash — about $100 for a pair of loafers and $15 for a lighter — to Ms. Van Rootselaar, as well as dispensing technical advice on how to carry out the attacks.

The suspect, identified by the police as James Cody Bryant, of Bellingham, Wash., was arrested on Tuesday morning, the authorities said at a Seattle news conference. Officials said that the suspect, who was born male and was referred to by authorities with male pronouns, identifies as female, similar to the shooter, Ms. Van Rootselaar.

The suspect’s lawyer, Gregory Murphy of the Federal Public Defender’s Office in Seattle, declined to provide a comment.

Ms. Van Rootselaar and the suspect met about three years ago on Omegle, a chat website that connects strangers. After the website shut down in 2023 amid criticism that it was a haven for sexual abuse, the pair kept in touch, said Mike Harrington, a special agent in charge of the F.B.I. Seattle field office.

Their friendship developed over conversations about planning the shooting that began at least six months before the attacks, including communication on Discord, a social media platform. Ms. Van Rootselaar was also active on various other social media accounts, where she documented her fascination with firearms and her mental health issues, for which she took prescribed medications and experimented with psychedelic drugs and other illegal substances.

The suspect, the authorities said, helped Ms. Van Rootselaar test livestreaming equipment, promised to help distribute and amplify footage taken during shooting, and advised how to start the car that Ms. Van Rootselaar used to travel from her home to the school.

“Without Bryant’s misplaced loyalty and willingness to operate the livestream, we don’t ultimately know if the shooter would have gone through with the crime,” said Mr. Harrington, adding that he was disturbed by messages between the pair. He said that they were difficult to read, “in part because of the casual tone these two individuals used when discussing the mass taking of innocent lives.”

The suspect was committed to assisting Ms. Van Rootselaar and stayed awake after an overnight shift to test the livestream. But during the actual attack, the stream lasted only 20 seconds before failing and was seen only by the suspect, said Charles Neil Floyd, the acting U.S. Attorney for the Western District of Washington.

The shooting in Tumbler Ridge shattered the quiet community of 2,400 people, and the school was later demolished. In addition to the eight people who were killed, two students were critically injured but survived, including a girl who was shot three times at close range.

In the months since the shooting, more than 30 lawsuits have been filed against OpenAI, an artificial intelligence company headquartered in San Francisco, following revelations by The Wall Street Journal that the company had internally flagged Ms. Van Rootselaar’s ChatGPT account for violent comments. Despite internal debate about how to proceed, the company chose not to escalate the complaint to the Canadian authorities and instead shut down Ms. Van Rootselaar’s account, though she was able to activate another one.

British Columbia last month filed a lawsuit against OpenAI in California, asserting that the shooting could have been prevented if the company had taken timely action. Sam Altman, the chief executive of OpenAI, apologized to the province in the months after the attacks and reasserted his company’s commitment to A.I. safety regulation, though David Eby, the premier of British Columbia, said those conversations had since stalled.

item.title: What to Know About the Fears of a Plague Outbreak in Russia
item.description:
Is there an outbreak of plague in Russia?

The short answer: We don’t know. A woman who works in a remote Siberian lab that studies plague has died of pneumonia. The lab has been locked down and the Russian authorities aren’t saying much, which has fueled speculation and rumors.

There’s a lot that is still unclear. The Times has gathered all the available information and talked to experts to try to make as much sense of it as possible. (Spoiler alert: Don’t panic.)

Darya Shipilova, a 28-year-old employee of Irkutsk’s Anti-Plague Research Institute of Siberia and the Far East, died of a pneumonia with an unknown cause earlier this month. Her death prompted Russian health authorities to quarantine the hospital where she died, along with the institute’s staff and other people who were in contact with her.

Yes. The plague has been with us a very long time. There are still a few hundred cases every year, mostly in Madagascar and the Democratic Republic of the Congo, but also in the United States, Russia and other countries.

Many people know the plague as the “Black Death,” a pandemic that is thought to have killed at least a third of Europe’s population in the 14th century.

Yersinia pestis, the bacteria that causes plague, has infected humans for thousands of years, also circulating among rodents and other small mammals, which serve as long-term reservoirs, and fleas, which spread it.

The U.S. Centers for Disease Control recommends starting treatment as soon as plague is suspected — even before testing is complete — with oral or intravenous antibiotics such as gentamicin and ciprofloxacin for 10 to 14 days.

There are three main ways that plague can infect humans. Bubonic plague occurs when the plague-causing bacteria multiplies in the lymph nodes, usually after a bite from an infected flea. Septicemic plague occurs when the infection spreads to the bloodstream. The most virulent type is pneumonic plague, which causes a severe rapid-onset lung infection and can be spread through a cough or sneeze.

Left untreated, pneumonic plague can kill a victim within days. But all three types of plague respond well to antibiotics if they are taken quickly. Based on the information we have so far, most experts aren’t too worried.

“Unfortunately, young people can die from pneumonia, so that development alone wouldn’t be enough to raise concern,” said Dr. Tom Inglesby, an epidemiologist at the Johns Hopkins Center for Health Security. “What I do think is concerning is the Russian reaction so far.”

The lack of details from the Russian authorities has unnerved many around the world who remain scarred by the Covid-19 pandemic. At that time, it was an authoritarian government in China, where the virus originated, that covered up information.

“Something is not adding up about this situation,” said Jennifer Nuzzo, an epidemiologist at Brown University. “The worker should not have contracted a fatal infection if she had been wearing personal protective equipment and had received antibiotics immediately after her exposure.”

In the aftermath of Shipilova’s death, Russian authorities failed to clarify her whereabouts before her death or to address questions about whether an accident had taken place at the institute.

When health officials and the United States government began asking questions, the Russian authorities gave additional information.

Russia said yesterday that Shipilova had been vaccinated against the disease and no “emergency situations” had been identified at the lab. (There are several vaccines that protect against plague, but it’s not clear how effective they are.)

Russia’s health regulator also said there were “no epidemiological risks for the population of Irkutsk and the Irkutsk region.”

After an unusual infection like this, health officials often provide the genome sequence of the virus or bacterium involved. This helps researchers pinpoint exactly which pathogen is to blame and how to fight it.

Public health experts suspect that Russian officials have already sequenced the pathogen involved in Ms. Shipilova’s death, and they wonder why that information has not been made public.

“Without that, the risk is uncertain, and I think we should be putting pressure on Russia to share the genome sequence,” said Dr. Raj Panjabi, a physician and former White House biosecurity official.

The existence of an active biological weapons program in Russia, which has historically sourced strains from anti-plague institutes, has added to global concerns.

In an annual threat assessment this year, U.S. intelligence agencies said Russian scientists were continuing to develop new chemical and biological weapons capabilities. The State Department, in its arms control compliance report last year, said Russia maintained an offensive biological warfare program in violation of the Biological Weapons Convention.

The use of plague as a bioweapon may have an ancient precedent. In the 14th century, according to the writings of a Genoese notary, a Mongol army catapulted plague-infested bodies into the Crimean city of Caffa — though some experts have cast doubt on that account.

In the modern era, a defector from the Soviet Union’s bioweapons program once claimed his government stockpiled “dozens of tons of smallpox and plague” that could be loaded onto bombs and missiles.

Reporting by K. R. Callaway, Edward Wong, Chris Buckley, Oleg Matsnev Milana Mazaeva and Alina Lobzina

item.title: ‘Maricarmen,’ Whose Eviction Enraged Spaniards, Dies at 87
item.description:
María del Carmen Abascal, the 87-year-old woman whose eviction from her home two weeks ago prompted widespread protests in Spain and spurred the prime minister to call national elections, died on Wednesday.

“We regret to announce that Maricarmen passed away today,” her representatives said in a statement, using the shortened form of her given names, by which Ms. Abascal had become widely known across Spain. They did not give a cause of death.

Ms. Abascal was evicted on Sept. 23 from the Madrid apartment where she had lived for more than 70 years, after police broke down her door. She was carried out on a stretcher and admitted to a hospital suffering from exhaustion.

Days later, as her condition failed to improve, her lawyer reached an agreement with the company that owned the apartment that would have allowed her to return once she was discharged.

“This solution came too late,” said the statement, signed by the tenants’ union, her lawyer and her family. “An absolutely avoidable situation following an agonizing process.”

The eviction touched a nerve among Spaniards fed up with a housing crisis. Tens of thousands of people, many of them young, took to the streets for days across the country, protesting skyrocketing rents and evictions, and singing “we are all Maricarmen.” Hundreds have also camped in Puerta del Sol, Madrid’s most famous square, and have no plans to clear out.

“This is not an eviction, this is murder,” hundreds of demonstrators chanted in the square on Wednesday evening, according to footage from Spain’s public broadcaster.

How The Times decides who gets an obituary. There is no formula, scoring system or checklist in determining the news value of a life. We investigate, research and ask around before settling on our subjects. If you know of someone who might be a candidate for a Times obituary, please suggest it here.

The eviction also brought about the end of the minority government of the left-wing prime minister, Pedro Sánchez. He called snap elections for Nov. 29, after a housing bill he presented last week, aimed at restricting evictions and freezing rents, was rejected in Parliament by a majority of conservative legislators.

“My deepest sympathies to Maricarmen’s family and loved ones,” Mr. Sánchez said on social media. “A warm embrace as well to all of us who feel this loss as our own today.”

Born in 1938, Ms. Abascal worked as secretary for a pharmaceutical company, according to the newspaper El País. She retired in 1998 and spent her retirement walking around her leafy, affluent Madrid neighborhood close to the Retiro Park and taking care of paintings and porcelain pieces at home.

She had moved with her family to the apartment in the 1950s. Her father held the lease and later passed it on to his wife, who in turn transferred the rent-controlled lease to Ms. Abascal in 2005. “I cannot move to another village,” she said in an interview with The New York Times last year.

“My father died in that house, and my mother died in that house,” she added. “That’s my life. My life is there, and you can’t put the life of a person out on the street like that.”

In 2020, the property was bought by the company Urbagestión, which sought to more than triple her monthly rent, which had been 500 euros, or about $570, according to her lawyer, Beatriz Duro. That was far more than Ms. Abascal, living on a €1,450 monthly pension, could afford.

The owners of Urbagestión, who did not respond to a request for comment on Wednesday, have previously disputed the account of the rent increase and said Ms. Abascal was simply not legally entitled to remain under the rent-controlled lease.

The yearslong legal battle between them ended with Spain’s Supreme Court siding with the landlord and approving the eviction.

On Sept. 23, after three failed attempts in previous months, the police removed Ms. Abascal from her apartment, after clearing out hundreds of activists who had barricaded the building to shield her. Her case quickly drew international attention and prompted the national government to respond.

“I wasn’t able to defend my home, but I did fight so that others can learn to fight for theirs,” Ms. Abascal said from her hospital bed after the eviction.

Days later, amid growing pressure, Ms. Abascal’s lawyer announced that she had reached a deal with the building owner that would allow her to return home. Under the agreement, she would have received an eight-year lease with a monthly rent equal to 30 percent of her pension, or about $460.

Ms. Abascal’s eviction marked a “turning point” in Spain, putting housing at the center of the national debate, her representatives said. Spaniards, especially young people with low salaries, are finding it increasingly difficult to rent homes in many cities, as an influx of tourists, immigrants and wealthy foreign buyers adds to demand, while sluggish construction and a shortage of public housing constrain supply.

Spain has a housing shortfall of about 755,000 homes, according to the Bank of Spain.

Despite a sharp decline in evictions — to about 25,000 last year, from around 68,000 in 2014 — the issue remains politically delicate for the government, particularly after Mr. Sánchez promised before taking office to end them. The role of a real estate company in Ms. Abascal’s eviction also angered many on the left, who accuse private investment firms of driving up housing costs in Spain.

Mr. Sánchez blamed his conservative opponents for Ms. Abascal’s eviction, pointing to their role in defeating legislation in February that would have restricted evictions like hers.

The prime minister’s previous housing polices expanded tenants’ rights, but right-wing parties have argued that they hurt small property owners and encourage squatting. In 2025, the conservative regional president of Madrid, Isabel Díaz Ayuso, called Mr. Sánchez an “accomplice” of squatters.

On Tuesday, after calling snap elections following the defeat of his recent bill, Mr. Sánchez said his government would pass a similar measure through a smaller parliamentary body that remains active after Parliament is dissolved. He also called on voters to deliver a “progressive majority in Parliament,” framing the election in part as a choice between moneyed elites and everyday people.

“When Congress turns its back on what people are experiencing in the streets, the government cannot look the other way,” Mr. Sánchez said.

The full ramifications of Ms. Abascal’s eviction remain to be seen. The tenants’ union, along with labor unions, has called a general strike for November in response, and her case is likely to loom over the election campaign.

Ms. Abascal’s representatives, who asked that the family’s privacy be respected, said her death would strengthen their determination to “defend the right to housing and fight against speculators.”

“And above all, we will honor what she always asked of us,” the statement said: “Fight, keep fighting for what is yours.”

Lara Jakes contributed reporting.

item.title: For France’s Resurgent Far Left, Student Protests Are an Opening and a Threat
item.description:
He shook hands and posed for selfies. He brandished a protest sign. He accepted a hug from a young fan. He cheered after an enthusiastic, if somewhat tuneless, rendition of “La Marseillaise,” the French national anthem.

Jean-Luc Mélenchon, the combative leader of France’s far-left party, France Unbowed, seemed to relish his appearance at a mass demonstration of high school students in Paris on Tuesday. And why not?

For a left-wing firebrand who appeals to young people and heads an insurgent party built on grass-roots protest, the student-led demonstrations that have swept France are a golden opportunity. Coming seven months before a presidential election in which Mr. Mélenchon is a genuine contender, they could not be better timed.

Yet the demonstrations have occasionally escalated into violent clashes between the protesters and the police, which carries acute risks for a politician seeking mainstream acceptance. Mr. Mélenchon, 75, seems to recognize the danger, moderating his usually pugnacious statements after the French recoiled from images of tear gas and trash cans set aflame.

“I call on you, young people, wherever you may be, to embrace the discipline of the struggle,” Mr. Mélenchon said at a rally last week. He encouraged students to take to the streets but added a caveat. “You must use nothing but nonviolent methods of struggle,” he said.

Marching on Tuesday, Mr. Mélenchon wore a white armband, meant to signify his role as a gentle chaperone for the students — an authority figure who could calm the protesters if their youthful passions overflowed and protect them from the police if scuffles broke out.

French government officials, however, assert that Mr. Mélenchon plays neither role. Far from moderating the students, they accuse his party of fomenting the unrest for political gain. What began as an organic protest movement, these officials say, has been hijacked by France Unbowed, emboldening bad actors who want to burn trash cans and hurl fireworks at police officers.

“Why wear a white armband to better give a leg up to those wearing black balaclavas?” France’s prime minister, Sébastien Lecornu, said angrily on Tuesday to the party’s leader in the National Assembly, Mathilde Panot.

“The reality is that you are ambiguous about violence,” Mr. Lecornu continued, “because violence is part of your political plan to throw the country into chaos between now and the presidential election.”

Mr. Mélenchon, Ms. Panot and their colleagues flatly reject those charges. Ms. Panot said the violence was a result of heavy-handed police tactics and accused the government of treating young people like “military adversaries.”

Still, there is no question that the party’s leaders have walked an increasingly fine line since the students began blockading schools last month. They have endorsed the students’ list of grievances and championed their right to take to the streets. In some cases, they have even linked arms with them.

“Mélenchon is seemingly trying to occupy two positions simultaneously,” said Philippe Marlière, a professor of French and European politics at University College London. “Political amplifier of the revolt, and politically disinterested defender of a movement that supposedly arose spontaneously.”

Nobody embodies those contradictions more than Bally Bagayoko, a rising star of France Unbowed and mayor of St.-Denis, a working-class suburb north of Paris that has been the epicenter of the unrest.

Critics pounced on a brief television interview Mr. Bagayoko gave last week after turning up at an early blockade of a school. “Violence, at a certain point, can be legitimate,” he said, though he hastened to add that his message to the students was that it is always better to avoid violence.

A charismatic, one-time semiprofessional basketball player, Mr. Bagayoko, 53, has become a conspicuous presence at the blockades and rallies. Standing in front of Rosa Parks High School in St.-Denis last Thursday, he listened to students, defused arguments between them, held court with visiting journalists and even stomped out a small fire lit by a handful of disrupters.

Asked about the risk of violence, Mr. Bagayoko said, “Of course, here and there, there might be some dysfunction, some mistakes that are made. But these are the signs of young people, who are not necessarily experienced activists and who, in the heat of the demonstration, sometimes tip over the edge. That’s a fact, and it’s the reason why adults must be there.”

“Sir,” said a young man, interrupting the mayor to gesture toward clouds of smoke nearby, “there’s a fire.”

Mr. Mélenchon said the government had unfairly painted Mr. Bagayoko as an instigator rather than a protector. “When Bally pulls out a burning trash can so that it doesn’t set fire to the building, he’s the one who’s accused of setting the trash can on fire,” Mr. Mélenchon said at the rally on Sunday.

He has good reason to push back against that narrative. In recent polls, Mr. Mélenchon is projected to finish just behind the leading center-right candidate, Édouard Philippe, in the race to replace President Emmanuel Macron. The far-right candidate, Marine Le Pen, maintains a double-digit lead over both.

That would put Mr. Mélenchon within striking distance of advancing to the second round of the French election next spring, the closest he has come to victory in three previous presidential campaigns.

Though Mr. Mélenchon presents himself as an insurgent, he spent much of his career as a member of the Socialist Party, France’s main center-left party. He served as a minister under Socialist prime minister Lionel Jospin before leaving the party in 2008. He founded France Unbowed in 2016.

A one-time Trotskyist, Mr. Mélenchon offers simple solutions to complex problems — writing off part of France’s debt, for example. He said France’s debt-burdened government should spend more money on schools.

Analysts said Mr. Mélenchon benefited from a hunger among voters for root-and-branch change. But his party — commonly known as L.F.I., the acronym of its French name, La France Insoumise — faces deep resistance. Centrists say his economic policies lack credibility, while some of its leaders, including Mr. Mélenchon himself, have been accused of antisemitism. And then there are the worries about violence.

“Almost seven French people out of 10 say that France Insoumise is a party that stirs up violence,” said Antoine Bristielle, director of the Public Opinion Observatory at the Jean Jaurès Foundation, a left-leaning think tank in Paris.

That is a higher percentage than those who voice similar fears about the far-right party, the National Rally, Mr. Bristielle said. Even in “rebellious France,” he said, “it can be quite negative for them in electoral terms.”

Giulia Imbert and Ségolène Le Stradic contributed reporting.

item.title: Italy Approves Contentious Law Giving Bonus Seats to Election Winners
item.description:
Italian lawmakers on Thursday approved a controversial law that awards bonus seats in Parliament to election winners, a move supporters say will help prevent governments from collapsing and that detractors denounce as unconstitutional and antidemocratic.

Championed by Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni, who had threatened to resign should the legislation not pass, the new law gives a bonus to the winning party or coalition of an election: 70 seats in the lower house of Parliament and 35 in the Senate, provided the party or coalition reaches 42 percent in both houses. Italy has a 600-seat Parliament, with 400 seats in the lower house and 200 seats in the Senate.

Proponents of the law have nicknamed it “Stabilicum,” saying it will ensure a coalition’s ability to govern in a country notorious for short-lived governments. Critics call it “Melonellum,” saying the law was made by the current government to bolster its chances at re-election next year. After the vote, opposition lawmakers raised signs with the slogans: “Fraudulent Law” and “No to the Deception.” Critics have vowed to petition the Constitutional Court of Italy for a review.

Italian governments have a history of instability; there have been 68 of them since Italy became a republic in 1946, with the shortest lasting a mere 22 days in 1954. Last month, Ms. Meloni, who was elected in September 2022, set a record for leading Italy’s longest-serving government. She is in the last year of a five-year mandate.

“This electoral law provides very strong stability,” which “builds credibility, allowing our businesses to operate with much greater peace of mind, and giving our foreign partners reassurances,” said Andrea Di Giuseppe, a member of Ms. Meloni’s Brothers of Italy party. The law was “very important,” he said in an interview.

The measure has been the topic of heated debate for months, prompting protests and petitions from some civil rights groups and constitutional experts as well as intense discussion in Parliament, even within Ms. Meloni’s center-right coalition.

“It doesn’t deliver what it promises,” said Gianluca Passarelli, a professor of political science at Sapienza University. He described it as a “Frankenstein law” with no comparable counterparts in any democracy.

Critics say that the bonus will allow the winning coalition to have outsize power to make key decisions without negotiating with lawmakers, including appointing judges or the president, thus undermining the democratic process.

“The bonus modifies the balance of actual electoral votes,” said Professor Passarelli, warning that the law also introduced “institutional tension” among the country’s governing forces by shifting power to the executive and weakening Parliament.

Massimo Giannini, a left-leaning journalist and pundit, compared the law to one passed in 1923 that enabled Mussolini’s National Fascist party to take control of Parliament.

“One hundred and three years later, this pattern repeats itself. An electoral law with a massive majority bonus that shifts the balance of democracy,” Mr. Giannini said on his podcast.

Previous electoral laws — Italy has passed six since 1993 in attempts to achieve political stability — have sought to introduce a majority bonus. A 2005 electoral law that awarded extra seats was declared unconstitutional in 2013, when the Constitutional Court ruled that the bonus had not been contingent on reaching a minimum threshold.

Critics have raised other concerns as well, including a provision that coalitions name their candidate for prime minister before elections.

Mr. Di Giuseppe, the lawmaker, said such a measure “ensures clarity and transparency for our citizens.” But opponents of the law say that the choice of the prime minister is a prerogative of Italy’s president, who is elected by Parliament and has specific legislative and judicial powers.

They have also argued over a provision about voter preferences. Supporters of the law say it will reinstate voters’ ability to express preferences in each district for three candidates from a party list of six names; critics say that the lists have party-selected lead candidates, limiting voters’ ability to choose.

Furthermore, as most of the lead candidates are expected to be men, there are concerns that a gender imbalance in Parliament will grow.

“The vast majority of the Parliament is made up of men, and we know they will keep their power,” said Professor Passarelli.

Thursday’s vote was held in secret ballot.

Salvatore Vassallo, the director of the Bologna-based Istituto Carlo Cattaneo, a research foundation, said it was not a given that the center-right coalition had the votes to reach the 42 percent threshold. He noted that Ms. Meloni faced a challenge on her right from Roberto Vannacci, a retired general whose new party, National Future, has found growing appeal among hard-right voters.

“Both sides have a chance at winning,” Mr. Vassallo said, and the majority bonus was “in the interest” of any coalition that sought to govern without having to compromise when cobbling together a ruling majority.

item.title: India’s Cockroach Party Leader Carries Gen Z’s Demands. They Are Many.
item.description:
He uncorked a generation’s anger at a broken college entrance exam system.

Now, the Gen Z movement that Abhijeet Dipke birthed five months ago and called the Cockroach Janta Party has become a formidable finger in the eye of the Indian government.

The cockroaches’ latest aim is the resignation of the country’s chief election commissioner, over what they say is a politically motivated purge of 130 million voters from the election rolls.

This Saturday, in perhaps their biggest challenge to Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s administration, they are calling on supporters to defy a police ban and stage a mass protest in New Delhi.

“For the nation, its democracy and our future, let’s all come together,” Mr. Dipke, 31, said on social media Thursday, appealing to Indians of all generations and ideologies. “Irrespective of your political inclinations, march with the youth.”

In fact, India’s youth have many more grievances: failing schools, insufficient jobs, violence against women, a lack of government accountability. Their frustrations have been boiling for years. There are so many of them — 367 million people between ages 15 and 29, the world’s largest Gen Z cohort.

Mr. Dipke says he feels intense pressure.

“It’s like someone has dropped a baby at my doorstep,” Mr. Dipke said on a recent road trip to highlight the problem with public schools in the countryside. “It actually scares me, to be very honest.”

“People have too many expectations, too many hopes,” he went on. “It’s like people are expecting me to resolve everything at once.”

Mr. Modi has not commented on the cockroach protests, though criticism has come from senior politicians of his Bharatiya Janata Party, including the chief minister of Maharashtra state, Devendra Fadnavis, who said their “fake narrative” over the voter roll revision would not succeed.

For Mr. Dipke — and the cockroaches — the risks are enormously high.

In a country where space for dissent has shrunk, they could be crushed as quickly as they appeared. The Delhi police have detained hundreds of people who defied the ban and protested in Delhi this week.

The cockroaches’ four leaders are all under the age of 32, with no political experience. Signs of friction have appeared with the main opposition party, the Indian National Congress. Its leader, Rahul Gandhi, is holding another rally across the country, in Chennai, on Saturday.

The cockroaches already have one win under their belt: the rare ouster of a government minister in connection to the entrance exams. They seem to have emboldened many more Indians to speak out against the government. Over the last week, a range of groups, from left-wing student activists to conservative regional politicians, have rallied in several cities.

“We are just frustrated by everything. Everything” said Aayushi Gaikwad, 18, who traveled three hours by train to attend a cockroach protest in Mumbai last Friday.

It was her first time at a protest. Around her, thousands of people waved Indian flags. As evening fell, Mr. Dipke led the crowd in singing the national anthem.

Ram Guha, a historian and an outspoken critic of Mr. Modi, credited the cockroach leaders for puncturing the “invincibility of the Modi government.”

“They clearly have a raw courage,” he said.

Not long after they forced the resignation of the education minister in July, the cockroaches turned to India’s rural schools. A range of Instagram-worthy horrors awaited them at government schools. Clogged toilets. Broken water taps. Overheated tin sheds for classrooms. Rotten onions in a school kitchen. Children wading through floodwaters to reach school.

We joined Mr. Dipke as he visited a remote district in western Maharashtra state, called Nandurbar, where he had spent the first five years of his childhood before his family moved to a city.

For Mr. Dipke, fixing schools is personal.

He was born to a Dalit family, seen as low on the Hindu caste ladder. He attended private schools. But his cousins, whose parents were not as educated as his, attended rural government schools, and the contrast was obvious to him, even as a child. He sat at a desk; they sat on the floor. He drank filtered water; they sometimes had no water. He went on to Boston University for a master’s degree; they repaired cars or worked construction.

“That has been one of the most neglected things since independence. Government schools have never been given the attention they need,” he said.

At a residential girls’ school in a village called Sari, he learned there was no running water in the fourth-floor bathrooms. The girls hauled buckets of water up four flights of stairs.

At a primary school, he met the one teacher who taught a class of first through fourth graders. There was no electricity, and the girls had to fetch water for their bathroom from across a field. The boys had no toilet at all.

Vishwas Thakarey, the teacher, said he, like many teachers, had been diverted from the classroom because he had been told to work on the voter roll revision. (Teachers are often pulled away on other government duties.)

At another residential school an hour’s drive away, Mr. Dipke found a dormitory for girls made of tin walls and a tin roof. There were no beds, only thin cotton mattresses to lay out every night. Mr. Dipke compared it to “an animal shed.” “If there are no basic facilities, how can we expect a quality education?” Mr. Dipke said.

The schools in the area serve mostly Indigenous children, among India’s most neglected.

Some education advocates say that the cockroaches’ focus on school infrastructure is neither new nor especially useful to improving educational outcomes. The latest Annual Survey of Education Results, an independent assessment, found roughly 30 percent of eighth graders in rural schools struggle with second grade-level texts, and around half with basic arithmetic.

In a measure of his naïveté, and also his awareness of it, Mr. Dipke said he had not yet read the ASER reports. He said he would.

Nor was he schooled in the realities of Nandurbar. The district’s top administrator, Mittali Sethi, is. She is trying to fix the electricity system in Sari village, address its groundwater shortage, and train teachers in schools that have fallen behind.

She said she welcomed the attention on school conditions, whether it came from the cockroaches or not. “If someone has raised a problem and it’s a problem, I will fix them,” she said.

(Since Mr. Dipke’s visit, a district water engineer and a health official had visited the village, a local activist said.)

Education experts said they hoped the cockroaches would continue their schools campaign to shine a light on an issue politicians had long ignored.

“The kind of attention they’ve been able to bring to schools, no one I can think of has been able to do that for 20 years,” said Reetika Khera, an economist at the Indian Institute of Technology Delhi who has researched rural schools for decades.

Last May, Mr. Dipke saw that India’s top judge had referred to young Indians as “cockroaches.” On a lark, he came up with the idea of the Cockroach Janta Party. Its website welcomed the “lazy” and the “unemployed.”

The idea caught fire, thrusting him into the public eye after anger boiled over at the leaked exams. “We didn’t plan or strategize this movement at all,” he said.

He admits to being no expert, on education or anything else. He says he is not a veteran activist nor a skilled orator. His sister reminds him that he was so camera-shy that he refused to take selfies with her. Now everyone wants a selfie with him.

In Mumbai last week, he went, as hundreds of fans do daily, to gawk at the home of Shah Rukh Khan, a Bollywood actor who played a character Mr. Dipke has long admired — only to be stopped for a selfie by one of his own fans. More people were looking at Mr. Dipke today, the fan said, than at the actor’s house.

Mr. Dipke smiled sheepishly, looked at the house, and said, “Oh ho. I’m still a big fan of yours.” He promptly shared the video with his 5.9 million followers on Instagram.

The next day, he stood on a makeshift stage with his fellow cockroach leaders, speaking to a crowd of thousands with a copy of the Indian constitution in his hand.

“Finally someone’s asking for accountability. Finally not being scared,” said Madhur Manohar, 26, who joined the protest.

“For the longest, everybody’s had frustrations,” her friend, Surabhi Apte, 30, said. “They didn’t know how to channel it. It was only dinner conversations, where your parents were like, ‘Ignore it.’”

“This is finally us doing something,” Ms. Manohar added.

The hopes and frustrations of India’s young are on stark display. Yes there are some parallels to student protests in France. There’s one huge difference. India’s Gen Z is enormous: 367 million Indians are between the ages of 15 and 29.

item.title: U.K. and Israel Agree to a Scaled-Back British Mission in East Jerusalem
item.description:
British and Israeli diplomats reached a last-minute agreement to avoid the closure of the British Consulate building in East Jerusalem, Britain’s foreign secretary announced on Thursday, leaving behind a scaled-back diplomatic mission to Palestinians.

Israel threatened last month to shut the consulate, which has served as the center of British outreach to Palestinians for decades, in response to London’s decision to impose trade sanctions on Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank, which have been expanding rapidly.

Until Thursday, both countries appeared to be locked in a series of escalating retaliations. British officials had privately warned that the closure of the consulate would be met with retaliation that might include expelling a number of Israeli diplomats from London.

Instead, the two countries issued statements early Thursday morning that each declared the issue resolved but described the compromise they had reached in significantly different ways.

In his statement, the British foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, said that the consulate building would not close but would be renamed.

“Our Consulate General building will not be closing, and will be known as the U.K. Mission, Jerusalem, from today,” Mr. Miliband said. He noted that the new facility “is independent, operational, and will continue to deliver vital services and our work with the Palestinian people.”

Mr. Miliband said that Britain stood by the sanctions imposed on the settlements in the West Bank, which are considered illegal under international law.

“We do not accept that the government of Israel has the legal right to close the British Consulate General in Jerusalem, which has been there for nearly 200 years,” he added, pointing to Britain’s “longstanding view that East Jerusalem is occupied territory.”

He also suggested that the reduction in staffing at the building would be temporary.

“We will work in the coming months to build back up our presence,” he wrote.

Gideon Saar, Israel’s foreign minister, issued a very different statement, asserting that Israel had followed through on its threat.

“⁠The British Consulate in Jerusalem is ending its operations today,” he wrote on social media. “Accordingly, the sign of the British Consulate in Jerusalem has been removed.”

In Mr. Saar’s telling, what remains at the building will be “a task force of only seven diplomats,” and “their scope of activity will be very limited.”

Mr. Saar added that the British consul general and 19 other diplomats would be ending their assignments. Mr. Miliband said only that a number of British officials who had been stationed at the consulate had been “temporarily withdrawn” to ensure their safety.

Mr. Saar also said that British officials had been removed from an international support center in Gaza and that British officials would no longer be able to train Palestinian Authority forces in the West Bank.

Ahmad Majdalani, a member of the Palestine Liberation Organization’s executive committee, said Palestinian leaders in the West Bank were relieved that Britain would be maintaining a diplomatic mission in East Jerusalem.

“What is important for us is that there’s diplomatic presence and that it is able to maintain relations with the Palestinian leadership and provide consular services to Palestinian citizens,” he said.

The agreement came after Jonathan Powell, Britain’s national security adviser, traveled to Israel last week for meetings aimed at reaching a compromise that could avoid a more serious breakdown between the longstanding allies.

By the time Mr. Powell left Israel last week, it appeared that the Israelis had rejected his suggestions, according to three people familiar with the private discussions who talked about them on condition of anonymity. But negotiations between Israeli and British officials continued until late Wednesday night, according to one Israeli official who was briefed on the ongoing discussions.

Despite the differences in their statements, Britain and Israel agreed to coordinate their publication at 7 a.m. British time, the Israeli official said.

Within minutes of the announcement of the change, the Israeli Foreign Ministry distributed before and after pictures showing the consulate entrance with signs and then without signs by the door.

item.title: Indian Opposition Leaders Detained as Protests Over Voter Rolls Intensify
item.description:
Protests by Indian opposition leaders were broken up by police in New Delhi for a second day on Wednesday, with many lawmakers dragged off the streets, as anger over a revision of voter rolls that dropped more than 130 million names continued to intensify across the country.

Videos show Rahul Gandhi, a leader of the opposition Indian National Congress, being lifted by police and shoved into a bus as he struggled to fight them off. His sister Priyanka Gandhi Vadra, also a member of Parliament, was seen holding a copy of the Indian Constitution as she lay on the road with other lawmakers before security forces dragged them away, in video posted by the National Congress on social media.

Hundreds of opposition lawmakers, led by Mr. Gandhi, have been trying to march on the country’s election commission since Tuesday. They accuse Gyanesh Kumar, the chief commissioner, of disenfranchising millions of Indians to benefit the ruling party.

But the lawmakers have been blocked by police, who have declared the protests illegal. On both days, columns of security forces surrounded the lawmakers and briefly detained many of them. The police have not commented on the detentions.

The lawmakers joined a broader movement of nationwide demonstrations that began on Friday over the voter-roll revision, called the Special Intensive Revision, or S.I.R. While the commission has framed the exercise as an effort to clean up voter lists, critics say the chaotic process has removed legitimate voters and burdened people with confusing document requirements in an attempt to entrench the power of Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s Bharatiya Janata Party, or B.J.P.

The B.J.P. has denied that it is trying to influence the revision, calling the protests the actions of sore losers who lost to Mr. Modi’s party in recent elections.

On the first day of the lawmakers’ protests, they and their supporters were blocked from reaching the election commission by a large security force. They then made a dash for the state radio broadcaster, where they sat in its yard for hours before the police moved in and bused away many to detention.

On Wednesday, the opposition leaders appeared to use a lunch as a diversion to fool police, but the ruse failed. After gathering at a restaurant for southern Indian delicacies of idli and dosa, they tried to make their way to the nearby Jantar Mantar, a site in the capital where protesters are normally allowed to gather, but the police reacted to detain many of them.

“There is no protest site left in the capital city of India. Do we protest from our homes?” said Harish Chandra Meena, a lawmaker from the Indian National Congress who marched on Wednesday but was not detained. “We were being manhandled like criminals.”

Protests have swept across India since Friday after an Indian newspaper reported that two members of the election commission lodged objections to moves made by Mr. Kumar during the voter revision process.

Earlier in the week, student protesters who were also trying to reach Jantar Mantar were met by a similar show of force, with many of them rounded up by police and herded into buses. Security around Mr. Kumar’s residence has been tightened, Indian media reported.

The issue is boiling toward a possible showdown this weekend. The Cockroach Janta Party, the Gen-Z backed movement that organized mass protests over an exam leak scandal over the summer, and other youth groups are calling for demonstrations in the capital on Saturday to demand the resignation of Mr. Kumar.

Mujib Mashal contributed reporting.

item.title: At a Potato Festival, Our Berlin Reporter Deepened His Ties to a New Land
item.description:
My little boy dragged his fingers through the dry soil of the land of his birth. They closed over a small yellow tuber, which he pulled from the dirt and lofted with a curious smile.

It was the sort of crisp September day when, in years past, his older brother and sister had traipsed through Virginia orchards — an autumnal tradition that our family was missing in Germany. But our youngest had never been to America, so we’d found the most German version we could imagine for him, at a farm called Domäne Dahlem.

Kartoffelfest.

“It’s like apple picking,” Lily, my wife, had explained. “But with potatoes.”

It felt like an outing our family needed, for reasons related to the challenges of being a foreign correspondent — and of raising a boy born into a culture that his parents and siblings are only slowly beginning to understand.

Our Berliner baby arrived in the spring of last year, soon after we settled here. We named him Hugo, which seemed both German and American. Much of his childhood has mirrored his older siblings’. He sleeps in his 5-year-old sister Nora’s hand-me-down crib and rides in her old stroller. Like his college-student brother, he listens to Wilco and Taylor Swift. He sometimes watches Dodger games beside me, though they start much deeper into the night here.

But Hugo is also, even with American parents and an American passport, a product of Germany. We’re trying to nurture his ties to it.

This is my — and my family’s — first foreign posting. It’s a big change from Washington, where I reported for 17 years. As I build sources and interview strangers, I’ve tried to decode Germany as a newcomer. And at a time of heightened national concern over immigration, my family has tried to pursue, to the best we can, the sort of assimilation that German voters across the political spectrum say they expect from new arrivals.

That includes learning the language and customs, and trying to adapt our traditions to our new home.

It’s especially true with Hugo. His day care is bilingual. We read him books in English and German. He responds to both languages, though we can’t always tell which he’s speaking.

Harvest season seemed ripe for more cultural communion. But what sort? Hugo had already been to one Oktoberfest, at 6 months old, and a Munich trip wasn’t in the cards this year.

It was a little early for pumpkins, and we were still laughing from last year’s visit to a country farm stand for jack-o’-lantern fodder. We’d piled several onto the counter to pay. The proprietor asked what soup we planned to make. She was bewildered when we told her we planned to carve a jagged smile into a perfect culinary gourd.

You know that saying, as American as apple pie? The German analogue is probably potatoes. People eat about 140 pounds of them per year here, double the global rate. It’s a surprise when a German meal arrives without one, baked or boiled or fried.

So it seemed only right to take Hugo and his sister on a city train to a plot of old farmland in the south of Berlin, for a potato celebration that draws thousands of visitors each year.

There we found stalls of crafts and food: potato pancakes, potatoes in the creamy cheese Germans call quark. Fries, of course. A fire pit to roast spuds like marshmallows on a skewer. A small biergarten, a tractor-themed play area, a horse-drawn carriage giving rides through the fields. Head scarves and trucker hats, children speaking German and Polish and English, a cross-section of the Berlin community, including lots of newcomers like us, trying to fit in.

The main event was in the fields. Hugo loved the real tractor — green, but not John Deere — that lumbered down the rows, churning up dirt and ejecting red, blue and yellow potatoes from a sort of metal grill trailing behind. Children followed from a safe distance, snagging its treasures like candy spilling out of a big-wheeled piñata.

“Whoaaaaaa,” Hugo said.

He helped his sister scoop potatoes into a burlap sack. Maybe too many. We pulled some from the bag and laid them back in the rows, catch-and-release style.

Other children picked them up. One shared our son’s name. A slightly older Hugo, also American, also living in Berlin. He said he didn’t like potatoes, but here he was.

“I had never heard of a Kartoffelfest before,” his mother, Helena Jaramillo, who moved here from Philadelphia, told me. “It seemed German enough to try something new.”

She seemed pleasantly surprised: “Seeing so many people excited about something so ordinary,” she said, “that’s what makes it fun.”

Waiting to weigh our haul, I heard a German couple marvel at how inexpensive it was, compared with similar organic produce at the grocery or farmer’s market. Maybe we wanted those extra potatoes back, after all?

Hugo, strapped to my chest in a toddler carrier, spied the tractor again. “Whoa!” he said.

In another field, I met Germans whose own fall traditions revolved around the potato festival. Vincent Schwalgun, 38, listed the ways his family would cook the many pounds they had gathered, and he told me why he’s come back for several years.

“To see my children happy,” he said, and “all dirty.”

I heard that some hard-core attendees arrive right when the gates open Saturday morning, to pluck the best of the rare varietals from one of the fields. I saw other families dressed like potato pros, in matching rubber boots and gardening gloves, carrying small shovels.

We took notes for next year.

We made our way back to the playground, wading through crowds. Our children climbed on the pretend tractor. My wife and I drank beers. As the sun fell, we carried Hugo home on the train, along with his sister and nearly five pounds of potatoes, surrounded by a chorus of other little Berliners.

I glanced down at our boy. He was dirty, and he was happy.

item.title: The Wave of Student Protests Roiling France
item.description:
Protests by high school students have rattled France in recent weeks, with hundreds of school blockages, large demonstrations and violent clashes with the police.

The students are protesting overcrowded classrooms, teacher shortages and decrepit buildings. The French government is scrambling to address their frustrations, which erupted amid a heated political climate ahead of a presidential election in April and have threatened to swell into a broader wave of grievances.

More than 700 police officers and more than 300 students and school staff members have been injured, some of them seriously, according to the government. Some high schools were set on fire or ransacked, and hundreds more were damaged, according to the education ministry.

The government has tried to assuage students’ anger, in part by pledging to create emergency plans to address school staffing shortages. But deteriorating public finances have left officials without much wiggle room to address the students’ complaints, and concessions have done little to calm the protesters.

item.title: In Trump’s Russian Oil Deal, Middle East Funds Are the Biggest Owners
item.description:
The Trump administration argues that its proposed multibillion-dollar Russian oil deal would advance American foreign policy interests and lower energy prices.

But most of the ownership in the deal would go to a group of Middle Eastern investors, including some with business ties to key U.S. officials involved in the negotiations, according to people familiar with the talks.

The deal, for a worldwide portfolio of oil fields, refineries and gas stations now owned by the sanctioned Russian energy giant Lukoil, has become intertwined with the U.S. talks with Russia over ending the war in Ukraine, The New York Times reported last week.

The United States government, through the U.S. International Development Finance Corporation, would get a stake of about 15 percent in the deal, without investing any cash up front, the people said.

The leader of the investor group, Todd Boehly, an American billionaire who has donated $2 million to pro-Trump causes in the last two years, would get a smaller minority stake.

But more than half of the equity will be cumulatively held by investors in the Middle East, according to three participants in the negotiations. The investors include entities tied to the royal family in Abu Dhabi and to two billionaire Syrian-born Qatari brothers, who are business partners with Jared Kushner, the president’s son-in-law, and Ivanka Trump, the president’s daughter.

The deal is structured in such a way that the United States — through Mr. Boehly and the government — would control a majority of the board of the resulting entity, some of the people close to the deal said. A senior administration official said the deal included a “substantial upfront payment and profits interest for the United States,” would enhance American “energy dominance” and outlast the current administration.

The Boehly group would acquire Lukoil stock with a face value of about $10 billion from non-Russian owners, although these purchases would be made at a significant discount, according to participants in the negotiations.

Once the purchase agreement is complete and approved by the Treasury Department, the assets would no longer be affected by U.S. sanctions on Lukoil, instantly driving up their value.

This deal is still in flux and could fall apart, but one of the previous bidders — the private equity fund Carlyle, based in Washington — is no longer actively pursuing the deal, after the U.S. government failed for months to sign off on Carlyle’s bid, according to parties involved in the deal talks.

The foreign-majority ownership raises new questions about who stands to most benefit from this complex transaction, which has involved negotiations with officials from the White House and the Kremlin, as well as a still-opaque list of investors from across the world.

President Vladimir V. Putin of Russia brought up the deal when he met at the Kremlin last month with Mr. Kushner and Steve Witkoff, a real estate developer, who both serve as Mr. Trump’s special envoys on the war in Ukraine. In Moscow, Mr. Putin is widely seen as having final say on the deal, even though Lukoil is a private company; in Washington, the Trump administration will need to approve it because of last year’s U.S. sanctions on Lukoil.

Whether or not the deal goes through, the behind-the-scenes negotiations over Lukoil show how Mr. Witkoff and Mr. Kushner have mixed their high-stakes diplomacy with talks that could provide a windfall to their business allies.

There is no indication that Mr. Kushner and Mr. Witkoff themselves stand to profit. The senior administration official said that the only interest guiding Mr. Kushner and Mr. Witkoff was “what is in the best interest of the American people.”

The deal’s proponents argue it would also be a windfall to U.S. taxpayers and a boon for U.S. interests because of the strategic assets in the deal, including key refineries in Eastern Europe. And the Trump administration has argued that showing Mr. Putin that the United States is prepared to do more business with Russia could help persuade him to compromise and end his war in Ukraine.

But for Mr. Putin, analysts say, the Lukoil sale has presented a chance to follow through on a strategy he has pursued ever since Mr. Trump returned to office: to use the promise of U.S.-Russia business deals to dissuade the White House from putting more pressure on Moscow over Ukraine.

Even better, from the Kremlin’s perspective, is that Mr. Kushner and Mr. Witkoff have business ties to two of the Middle Eastern investors involved in the deal, analysts say.

“The national security interests of the U.S. and U.S. allies, and private interests, are just so conflated,” Alexander Gabuev, director of the Carnegie Russia Eurasia Center, said. “That’s exactly the muddy waters that Putin and his K.G.B. negotiating school are thriving in.”

As Mr. Putin escalates his bombardment of Ukraine, Mr. Gabuev went on, “Lukoil just helps him to buy time.”

In the United Arab Emirates, one of the major investors is led by Sheikh Tahnoon bin Zayed Al Nahyan. He is a powerful member of the Abu Dhabi royal family whose business ventures have also invested in Mr. Kushner’s private equity fund and in World Liberty Financial, the cryptocurrency company co-founded in 2024 by Mr. Witkoff, as well as his and Mr. Trump’s sons. The White House has said that Mr. Witkoff has divested his position in the company.

In Qatar, the deal’s investors are the billionaire Syrian-born brothers Ramez and Moutaz Al-Khayyat, who are partners of Mr. Kushner and his wife, Ivanka Trump, in a proposed multibillion-dollar luxury Mediterranean coast resort in Albania.

The Khayyats and their Doha-based conglomerate have moved rapidly over the last year to expand business deals in the energy sector, including the oil industry, with investments now in Syria, Iraq, Libya and most recently in Venezuela.

The family has close ties to the royal family of Qatar dating back more than a decade, including with Sheikh Suhaim Bin AbdulAziz Al Thani, who serves on the boards of two of the Khayyats’ ventures.

Carlyle in January separately secured a “nonexclusive” purchase agreement, with a plan to put the payment at least temporarily into a locked up U.S. bank account, to avoid bringing profits to Russian investors who own Lukoil. But it then did not get the sign off it needed to complete the deal.

Some of the people close to the deal said the Carlyle deal was a nonstarter for the Russians, since they did not expect that the United States would ever release the money kept in a U.S. account.

These talks among possible buyers including Carlyle and Mr. Boehly started late last year after the Trump administration imposed sanctions on Lukoil, in an effort to force the end of the war in Ukraine. Lukoil’s international assets are spread across Europe, Africa, Mexico and the Middle East, and also include about 200 gas stations along the Mid-Atlantic coast of the United States.

The deal would need approval from the Treasury’s Office of Foreign Assets Control, which has set as a precondition for lifting the sanctions that any transfer of the assets “not provide a windfall to Lukoil,” since the United States does not want to deliver profits back to Russia.

The move by the United States government to impose sanctions on a foreign company and then play a direct role in moving to buy these sanctioned assets is extremely unusual, according to two former federal officials involved in sanctions efforts.

“I cannot recall any remotely similar arrangement in the 20 years I’ve focused on sanctions,” said Jeremy Paner, a former Treasury Department sanctions lawyer who now handles corporate sanctions compliance efforts.

In a statement, an official with the U.S. International Development Finance Corporation said the proposed deal was good for the United States, as it “would advance the Trump administration’s commitment to strengthen U.S. economic security, advance U.S. foreign policy and lower energy prices for everyday Americans.”

The Trump administration, at least initially, would not put money into the deal, people familiar with the deal said, but the United States will still be in line to secure profits.

Once the sale of the Lukoil international assets is complete, the buyers plan to spend hundreds of millions of dollars to expand and retrofit different parts of these operations.

The negotiations are delicate, the people said, because Mr. Putin could still reject it if he sees it as unduly benefiting the United States. That is why, they said, the participation of Middle Eastern investors is important, since the Kremlin sees Qatar and the Emirates as friendly countries.

“Look at what’s happening to Lukoil,” Mr. Putin said at a conference last week, accusing the West of “the theft of our companies.”

The Treasury Department has set an Oct. 22 deadline for the negotiations over the sale. That deadline might be extended again, but on Wednesday two U.S. senators sent a letter to Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent insisting that they ensure no financial benefits go to Russian players if the Lukoil sale is approved.

“Every day that passes without maximum economic pressure allows Moscow to sustain this military escalation,” read the letter from Senator Roger Wicker, Republican of Mississippi, the chairman of the Senate Armed Services Committee, and Senator Jeanne Shaheen of New Hampshire, the top Democrat on the Senate Foreign Relations Committee.

Dmitri S. Peskov, Mr. Putin’s spokesman, declined to comment on the Lukoil sale process when asked about it in his daily conference call with reporters on Monday.

“I will only say that, indeed, the topic of interacting and cooperating in the energy sector is indeed being raised in conversations with American counterparts,” Mr. Peskov said.

Ana Swanson, Tyler Pager, Ivan Nechepurenko and Andrew E. Kramer contributed reporting.

item.title: Debating the Risks Posed by Artificial Intelligence
item.description:
This article is from a special report on the Athens Democracy Forum, held in association with The New York Times, where experts gathered in the Greek capital last week to discuss global issues.

Lorena Austin, a U.S. Democrat elected to Arizona’s House of Representatives in 2022, fights for issues such as housing and homelessness, education and climate.

Yet for a brief moment in September, voters were left with a completely different impression of her.

In a social-media campaign ad (posted by the conservative advocacy group Turning Point Action), a smiling Ms. Austin was pictured alongside a group of Democrats supporting the other side: the conservative Republican candidate Andy Biggs, who is running for governor of Arizona in November.

The image was pure fabrication.

Technology and its threats to democracy were the central theme of last week’s Athens Democracy Forum, an annual gathering of policymakers, business leaders, academics and activists held in association with The New York Times.

The case of Ms. Austin’s fake photo came up in a presentation by William Gates, executive director of the Mechanics of Democracy Laboratory at Arizona State University, who gave it as an example of the mounting dangers to democracy from disinformation created by artificial intelligence.

He was hardly alone. At the Athens gathering, one panel after another warned of the potential risks that social media, deepfakes, cyberattacks and the rapid advances of A.I. posed to society, democracy and humanity as a whole.

Other key topics at this year’s forum: the United States’ ongoing war with Iran, and the aftermath of the Nov. 3 U.S. congressional elections.

In an interview after his presentation, Mr. Gates acknowledged that lying about your opponent has been going on for as long as we’ve had politics.

But what has changed, he said, was how fast troublesome fakes could be created. He pointed out that in the past, creating a fake photograph was a time-consuming job requiring a graphic designer and a good deal of expertise. Not today, he said. All it took today was asking A.I. to do it for you.

But the damage can be extensive. In a fake video, for example, an election official might declare that an election has been canceled, urging voters to stay home, Mr. Gates said; or announce that 50 polling stations have closed, sending voters to nonexistent locations.

As in previous years, the forum gave voice to the young — university students as well as teenagers — to ensure that the discussions were of relevance to their generation.

One youth-related panel focused on teen access to social media, following Australia’s decision last December to ban children under 16 from having accounts on major social media platforms.

Speaking in favor of controls was Peter G. Kirchschläger, a professor of ethics at the University of Lucerne in Switzerland and a visiting professor at ETH Zurich. He said young people, now “addicted” to social media, needed “rehab measures.”

“We would never distribute cigarettes to 10-year-olds and say, ‘Look: find a responsible way to deal with tobacco,’” he said.

He called for “preventive measures” and social-media education to ensure that young people would “use these technologies in a responsible way.”

But Alexia Kadoglou, a teenage student, said she was against social media bans, because she used social media every day to communicate with her friends, keep up with the news and express herself.

“We should have access to social media without any restrictions, but we should learn how to be digitally responsible,” she said. “Young people should have a say.”

Besides their harmful impact on adolescents, the internet and social media have also done demonstrable damage to journalism: Readers have migrated online, and revenues from advertising and print subscriptions have dwindled. Now, A.I. is throwing up a whole new set of challenges, said speakers in a panel on rethinking journalism.

“It’s an enormous threat to our industry,” said Martin Baron, a former executive editor at The Washington Post. He said many people got their news from chatbots, which they trusted more than news organizations because they assumed the news was gathered from all sources and was not biased in any way. And yet, he said, “A.I. can often produce really inaccurate results.”

Eliza Anyangwe, former editor in chief of Fuller, a global nonprofit news organization reporting on women and gender-diverse people, said that when reporting on A.I., journalists often gave ample voice to the heads of the big tech companies and ended up “amplifying the same tropes” and messages that the technology bosses were putting out.

“The challenge of dealing with A.I. is: How do we maintain some distance of it, where we are critical of it, where we take a breath to think and where we are engaging audiences” and asking if they understand what A.I. is, she said.

The powers and perils of A.I. were spelled out in detail by The Times’s columnist Thomas Friedman, who is writing a book about the technology.

In an opening-night address, he described it as “the second Big Bang” that had been “set off by us: We have become godlike as a species.”

He said humankind had, through the advances of science and technology, created an artificial brain, changed the climate, generated an entirely new interconnected galaxy called cyberspace, produced weapons that could destroy the planet, and allowed the convergence of quantum computing, fusion energy and A.I.

“We now have the power to part the Red Sea. Just one problem: without the Ten Commandments,” said Mr. Friedman in an address held inside the neoclassical headquarters of the Academy of Athens.

“The first challenge for democracies is going to be to collaborate globally” and “collectively write these together,” he said. It was, Mr. Friedman added, a do-or-die necessity: “We are going to rise together, or we’re going to fall together.”

That prognosis was echoed by Finance Minister Kyriakos Pierrakakis of Greece, who in a subsequent conversation urged the world’s governments to get together to regulate A.I.

No country in the world is big enough to govern A.I. alone, not even the U.S. or China, said Mr. Pierrakakis, a graduate of Harvard University and of the Massachusetts Institute of Technology. “We need global governance.” Governments are “not yet fully up to speed with the change that is happening,” and with the velocity of that change. What previously took years or decades now happens in months or even weeks, said Mr. Pierrakakis, who previously served as Greece’s Minister for Digital Governance.

He said institutions are “the software of our democracy” and concluded that “the software needs to change to adapt to the A.I. era.”

As ever at the forum, geopolitics and international conflicts were in the spotlight. This year’s focus was Iran — which the United States and Israel attacked on Feb. 28, decapitating its leadership. Since then, Iran has led missile and drone attacks on countries and ships in the region, pushing up oil prices.

Speaking on the Iran panel, Mr. Friedman from The Times predicted that the conflict would end in a U.S.-Iran negotiation, but “given the weak position the Americans have now, the negotiation will end in Iran’s favor. We cannot end this war, we the United States, without giving a new lease on life to the Islamic Republic in the near term.”

Nazenin Ansari — managing editor of the digital publications Kayhan London and Kayhan Life, read by the global Iranian community — said: “The survival of the Islamic Republic and the well-being of the Iranian people are profoundly different things.”

She said that while international attention is focused on the Islamic Republic, the Iranian people, “whose voices are so often missed,” are enduring economic hardship and severe repression.

item.title: The Leader Thailand Could Have Had
item.description:
This article is from a special report on the Athens Democracy Forum, held in association with The New York Times, where experts gathered in the Greek capital last week to discuss global issues.

Pita Limjaroenrat would have become Thailand’s prime minister at age 42 had his country been a parliamentary democracy such as Britain.

Mr. Pita led his Move Forward party to a surprise first-place finish in the May 2023 elections after campaigning to upend the status quo. His platform included legalizing same-sex marriage, setting a $13 minimum wage and slashing the army’s budget. Having won the backing of more than 14 million voters, he declared, “A new day for the people has arrived,” and formed an eight-party coalition that would allow him to govern. Yet under Thailand’s constitutional system, Move Forward failed to get enough support in the military-backed Senate to take power. By August 2024, the party had been disbanded, and Mr. Pita had been banned from politics for 10 years.

Today, Mr. Pita is back on a campus he knows well: Harvard University’s Kennedy School of Government, where he completed a Master in Public Administration in 2011. This time he is teaching. He was a speaker last week at the Athens Democracy Forum, an annual gathering of policymakers, business leaders, academics and activists held in association with The New York Times. In a video interview before the forum, he discussed the future of democracy in Thailand, and how he is grooming his students to run for office in their own developing nations. The conversation has been edited and condensed.

You came very close to becoming Thailand’s prime minister three years ago. How do you feel, looking back on things today?

I’m very worried, because this could happen again in the future. Thailand is a competitive autocracy, where autocrats allow you to have elections once in a while. But they can always overturn the people’s choice in various ways.

Until two decades ago, autocrats were not very smart. They had to put tanks on the street, have warfare and violence on the street to seize power. In the last two decades, they have become much smarter, and mastered discreet ways of suspending people, banning politicians, dissolving political parties. So there’s no need for them to put tanks on the street.

In Thailand, we’ve been democratic for about 100 years. And yet we have had 13 military coups in that time. Every seven years [on average], a military coup will intervene and pause democracy.

Thailand is a country that is punching below its weight. We are the second-largest country in ASEAN [Association of South East Asian Nations]. Yet we’re among the slowest growing.

Are you living between the U.S. and Thailand at the moment?

I spend most of my time in Boston now, at the Harvard Kennedy School, where it all began. I’ve come full circle: from turning textbooks into reality, I have gone to turning reality into textbooks. I teach how to run for public office in developing countries.

What would be an ideal future in Thailand from your perspective?

I want to be able to compete in a free and fair election once again, and win again, with the support of the majority of the people — including the younger generation.

The platform we ran on in 2023 was a 3-D platform: It called for a demilitarized, demonopolized and decentralized Thailand. We campaigned for a country with no more coups, a country where the big conglomerates don’t have power over markets, and a country where Bangkok is not Thailand, and Thailand is not Bangkok.

What are you doing at Harvard?

I am grooming next-generation leaders, and spending time with young people from ASEAN countries. They’re 18, 19 or 20, and I have office hours for whoever wants to run for public office.

That’s the power bank that keeps me energized. We have a younger generation emerging, and new voters at every election cycle.

Can you be more specific about what you teach at Harvard, and what feedback the students give?

The class is called “How to run for public office in developing countries” — becoming a politician. I took the class when I was a student at the Kennedy School, and the man who taught it was Steve Jarding, a campaign manager for Bill Clinton. I used it to run for office in Thailand in 2023.

What did Steve Jarding teach you?

How to run for public office and articulate why you want to run in the first place. You learned the whole upstream, midstream, and downstream of running for office: what your campaign structure is, how you do route management, how you knock on doors, how you fund-raise. We practiced organizing campaign rallies, delivering stump speeches.

Today, I’m returning to teach based on the reality in developing countries. This is democracy in hard places. It’s not American-style democracy.

How have you adapted what you learned at Harvard two decades ago, and what are you bringing to the table that’s different?

The framework is quite similar, but it has obviously been updated because of technology and social media: fake news, deepfakes and misinformation — as well as the use of artificial intelligence in campaigns, slogan design, or fund-raising.

So you teach students about the ugly side of technology — fake news, deepfakes, misinformation — but also its positive side?

Yes. Artificial intelligence can be used in slogan design, fund-raising plans, route optimization: how you spend the day and meet as many people as you can. It can be used in segmentation, in running data-driven campaigns, in precision politics. For example, you separate people into red, yellow, and green groups. If it’s green, they meet me one time. If it’s red, I don’t show up. If it’s yellow, they meet me three times.

Who are your students, and what’s their reaction to what you teach?

They’re from countries such as Colombia, Chile, Japan, the Philippines, Indonesia, Singapore, and Thailand. And there’s a verbal MOU whereby they promise me that they will run for office after graduation — within five years.

I grill them: Do you know what office you want to run for? Do you want to be a mayor, a governor or a member of parliament? If they show up not knowing what they want to do, then I give more attention to the students who have a concrete plan and a very concrete idea.

So far, so good. I think they have a good, solid plan crafted for them for free, so that when they finish working for Boston Consulting Group or J.P. Morgan or the like, and they finally have enough money to run, then they have this plan that they can go forward with. I’m trying to inject fresh blood into the system all around the world — as much as I can.
