item.title: A Photo of Mussolini’s Corpse Led Page 1. How It Got There Is a Tale.
item.description:
This story is part of a series marking 175 years of eyewitness journalism from The New York Times. Read more here.

It was an incredible thing to see firsthand: the battered bodies of the deposed Italian fascist leader Benito Mussolini and his lover, Clara Petacci, dumped like so much rubbish in a public square in Milan in the waning days of World War II. The New York Times correspondent Milton Bracker was there on that day, April 29, 1945 — nine days before VE day, the end of the war in Europe — to take the measure of the moment.

“Benito Mussolini came back last night to the city where his fascism was born,” Bracker wrote in a front-page article in the next day’s paper. “He came back on the floor of a closed moving van, his dead body flung on the bodies of his mistress and 12 men shot with him.”

Bracker’s account, written in the first person with an unusual undercurrent of moral indignation, reflected the gravity of the event, the sense that history had swerved suddenly in a new direction. It told how, his support crumbling away, Mussolini had driven north in an attempt to escape to Switzerland. Before he got there, Bracker wrote, he was caught, “like the fleeing Marie Antoinette.”

The story was packed with details. Mussolini’s speedy trial and summary execution by a firing squad along with a group of his followers in Giulino di Mezzegra, in northern Italy. How their bodies were heaped in a van and deposited in the Piazzale Loreto in Milan, of symbolic importance “because recently 15 patriots were executed there.”

The bodies were then savagely attacked by angry partisans. Bracker said he and other American reporters had been “thrust into the circle of death” by onlookers eager to show them what had happened.

An unknown photographer shows the reporter at the scene in his military uniform, notebook in hand, interviewing a soldier while the corpses of Mussolini and his mistress lay sprawled at their feet. Bracker saw two young men viciously kicking the slain dictator’s head, causing a “hideous crunch that wholly disfigured the once-proud face,” he wrote.

“It was naturally one of the grimmest moments of our lives, but it will at least serve to give absolutely authentic eyewitness accounts,” he added.

It is one thing to read about such an event in a newspaper; it’s another thing to see a picture of it. Bracker’s story was accompanied by a four-column, front-page photograph depicting the chaotic scene: the bodies of Mussolini and Petacci atop the pile of corpses — Mussolini is easily identifiable by his bald head — as a crowd of armed onlookers pushes and jostles alongside them.

The following day, May 1, the paper printed two additional photographs. One showed the corpses of Mussolini, Petacci and others dangling by their ankles from a pole at an abandoned service station, where they had been strung up by the mob; another showed Lieut. Gen. Achille Starace, an ally of Mussolini, in the final moments before his own execution by a firing squad.

The publication of these photographs was a coup for The Times. Transmitting photos around the world in the age of the internet is such a smooth undertaking that it’s easy to forget how difficult it once was. In the early days of news photography, the only method to get a photo from one place to another was to physically transport the film — an exercise in delayed gratification if, say, it involved a journey by boat across the Atlantic.

A breakthrough came in the 1920s with the development of practical radiophoto technology, a technique by which photographs were scanned and their tones converted into electrical pulses. The pulses were then sent wirelessly to New York, in the case of The Times, where they were transformed back into photographic images for publication.

Along with several other major news organizations, including The Chicago Tribune and The Christian Science Monitor, The Times in 1929 set up a company called Press Wireless that bypassed commercial telegraph monopolies. The company built its own shortwave radio transmission and receiving stations, allowing its members to transmit articles and images far more efficiently.

But transmission was still subject to logistical challenges, particularly during war. At the time of Mussolini’s death, the Press Wireless transmitting office nearest to Milan was in Geneva, some 155 miles away as the crow flies. So in order to get the photographs — which were taken by an Italian photographer whose name remains stubbornly lost to time — to New York, someone first had to get them to Geneva.

Bracker was busy writing his article, the first draft of history. But the mysterious photographer knew Daniel T. Brigham, a Times correspondent based in Bern, Switzerland, and offered to personally transport the photos to Ponte Chiasso, on the Italian-Swiss border, and put them on a train bound for Bern.

Even that was no easy task in a country ravaged by war. The photographer had to hitchhike to the border, navigating “highways blocked with bewildered countrymen and kept in ferment by roving partisan bands,” Meyer Berger, a former Times correspondent, wrote in his book about The Times’s first century, “The Story of The New York Times 1851-1951.” But the photographer got there and put the package on the train.

“Oh, boy, have I got something special!” Brigham exclaimed when he called The Times late that night to say that he had collected the package in Bern. He asked the Press Wireless office, normally closed on Sunday, to prepare to receive his transmission. Meanwhile, he got ready to go to Geneva.

After scrounging up gas for the trip, and obtaining permission from a military censor to use the photos, Brigham set off alone on a dangerous Alpine drive in the middle of the night. “He headed into a mountain blizzard, careening and skidding over black precipices on the dark and narrow alpine roads,” Berger wrote. At one point, one of his tires blew out, and Brigham had to change it in the storm.

At 11:30 p.m. New York time — 5:30 a.m. in Geneva — the images began to emerge from the Press Wireless’s receiver at The Times. They arrived too late for the first edition. But after some changes to the paper’s layout by the night managing editor, Raymond H. McCaw, the first photo, of Mussolini lying in the pile of corpses, was placed on the front page for the second edition.

It was rare to print such a graphic image in the paper, especially on the front page. But the photographs were irrefutable proof that Mussolini was dead. And they were a crucial visual complement to the story of what happened, told in Bracker’s accompanying article and analyzed in a Times editorial that same day.

“The wretched end of Benito Mussolini marks a fitting end to a wretched life,” the editorial said. “The man who once boasted that he was going to restore the glories of ancient Rome is now a corpse in a public square in Milan, with a howling mob cursing and kicking and spitting on his remains.”

After putting the paper to bed, McCaw typed out a memo to the publisher, Arthur Hays Sulzberger, with the time at the top, 1:15 a.m.

“Mr. Sulzberger: I think you will agree that the Mussolini picture was well worth Page 1,” he wrote. “Personally, I think that next to the Iwo Jima flag-raising this was the second-best picture of the year,” he added, referring to the famous photo, by Joe Rosenthal of The Associated Press, of six Marines raising the American flag on the island of Iwo Jima two months earlier.

Sulzberger’s Western Union message to Brigham in Bern later that day was presumably no less heartfelt, despite being written in the weird unpunctuated syntax peculiar to telegrams. “Congratulations securing Mussolini picture which unique,” he wrote.

item.title: Cecily Gemmell Has Died. She Was Churchill’s Last Surviving Secretary.
item.description:
Cecily Gemmell, Winston Churchill’s last surviving personal secretary, who took down the British prime minister’s speeches as he composed them aloud, died on Thursday in New York City. She was 97.

Her caretaker, Mary Pizzarelli, confirmed the death.

Ms. Gemmell, known as Chips, first entered Churchill’s orbit in the summer of 1947 at the age of 18, arriving in the still-stunned aftermath of his 1945 general election defeat as Britain’s wartime prime minister. His reputation as the man who had saved the world from Hitler’s tyranny was titanic, but his electoral ejection from No. 10 Downing Street before final victory — Germany had surrendered, Japan had not — remained humbling.

Youth was a requirement for a Churchill stenotyping secretary. “The Old Man,” as he was known, dictated so long and so late into the night, as a rule, that stamina was essential. Ms. Gemmell joined a team of extraordinarily bright and capable, if often exhausted, young women, and a proud line of exceptional Churchill personal secretaries (all but one of them female) that extended back through both world wars to 1902. At her death, Ms. Gemmell was the last.

Ms. Gemmell was ushered into Churchill’s presence for the first time at his new postwar London residence, 28 Hyde Park Gate. Churchill was just back from a hospital stay. His bed had been moved into the downstairs dining room and he was sitting up in it, smoking a cigar. The teenage Ms. Gemmell was on the verge of graduating from the venerable Mrs. Hoster’s Secretarial College, which the Churchills had long used as a kind of employment agency.

“I was terrified of him,” Ms. Gemmell later recalled, but he was “very benign.”

“‘How do you do, my dear?’ he asked. I think I shook his hand,” she recalled for the oral history project at the Churchill Archives. “He seemed so incredibly friendly that I felt emboldened to talk to him.” Jo Sturdee Onslow, Churchill’s secretary in chief, “had to rush me away,” she said. “But on that interview, my life started.”

Ms. Gemmell was initially assigned to Churchill’s literary assistant, Denis Kelly, cataloging the prime minister’s World War II papers in anticipation of Churchill writing his war memoirs. The cache was housed at Chartwell, Churchill’s country home in the county of Kent, and so a place was found for Ms. Gemmell to live in the nearby village of Westerham. She bicycled back and forth to Chartwell, pushing the bike up “an incredibly steep hill” that, at least, “was a cinch coming back down.”

She worked in what she described as the semi-basement of the Muniment Room at Chartwell — “completely untrained,” but tasked with organizing the monumental paper trail of Churchill’s wartime existence. She saw virtually no one other than Mr. Kelly, along with “everybody’s socks — the socks of the famous,” from her obscured vantage. She would “look up and see Anthony Eden’s pink socks leaving the room,” she recalled, referring to the foreign secretary who would later briefly become prime minister. “All I saw of the famous were their socks.”

The cataloging finally ended and, at last, Ms. Gemmell was summoned to work with Churchill himself one evening after dinner at Chartwell. “There he was,” she said, “sitting up in his four-poster bed in his little bedroom, with brandy and cigars, and there was a card table with a typewriter on it. ‘Good evening,’ he said. ‘Put your paper in.’”

Her initial efforts were shaky. “The nervousness of someone dictating right onto the typewriter was enough,” she later said in an interview, “but the fact that it was ‘him,’ and he was hard to hear, and I really couldn’t understand all he said, but I couldn’t stop and say, ‘I can’t hear you,’ and the typewriters, which were ‘silent’ — very little clack — had a very hard action, which made it very hard to type.

“I just kept thinking, ‘This is only a nightmare; I’m going to wake up, this isn’t real.’ And I think that thought kept me going.”

Cecily Gemmell was born in Bangalore, India, on Dec. 25, 1928. Her father, Col. Geoffrey Woodburn Gemmell, was a map surveyor in the Indian Army, second to the surveyor general. Her mother, Winifred Grace Hall, accompanied and assisted her husband on his field trips. “My mother managed the domestic side of things,” Ms. Gemmell recalled. “She loved camping and walking many miles a day. They were out in the jungles for a month or two at a time.”

Named for her father’s youngest brother, Cecil, who had been killed in France at the end of World War I, Ms. Gemmell would always be known to her family and friends by her uncle’s nickname, Chips. She was educated at The New School (known as Harrow on the Hooghly), which had been founded in Calcutta (now Kolkata) at the outset of World War II and then transported to Darjeeling, before disbanding in 1944.

The family returned to England in the summer of 1945. There, Ms. Gemmell completed her education at Mrs. Hoster’s — initially in Lincolnshire, where the school had been evacuated to during the war, before returning with the school to London.

Ms. Gemmell was back again in London with Churchill when he was returned as prime minister in 1951. She accompanied her boss to the Cabinet Room at 10 Downing Street; to the racecourses where his thoroughbreds ran; to Monte Carlo, where he gambled; to Blenheim Palace, where he was born; to Marrakesh, Lake Como and the Dolomites, where he painted.

One day Churchill asked Ms. Gemmell to sit for a portrait. It was quite an honor; he painted very few. Come Christmastime at No. 10, he planned to present the painting to her as a gift. “Do you know what you’re getting for Christmas?” he chortled, unable to keep his own secret. “You’re going to get your picture.”

Ms. Gemmell eventually volunteered to work for Churchill’s wife, Clementine, where the strain was considerably less. She retired from active Churchill duty in 1953 and moved to New York City, securing a high-level secretarial job at Life magazine.

She remained with Life for nine years, and worked at Time Inc. in a similar role for many years more. During this time, she became a habitué of the jazz clubs near her Midtown apartment. (“I never wanted the party to end,” she once explained, “and the jazz clubs stayed open the latest!”)

One night, Ms. Gemmell met the pianist John Bunch, a longtime accompanist of Tony Bennett’s, as well as a sideman with Benny Goodman. In the spring of 1977, she moved in with him. They were married on New Year’s Day 1998. Mr. Bunch died in 2010; no immediate family members survive.

Ms. Gemmell’s final year in the Churchills’ employ, 1953, was the year that Winston Churchill was knighted.

“I ran across him in a corridor at No. 10,” she later remembered. “I couldn’t think what to call him; I’d been ruminating about it, with some consternation. Finally, I blurted out, ‘Good morning, Sir Winston.’ He gave one of his wonderful sort of inward chuckles and I heard him quietly say, ‘Don’t be so cheeky.’”

item.title: U.N. Warns Against Technology Used to Read Citizens’ Minds
item.description:
The scenarios sound like science fiction: Police officers accessing data contained in suspects’ brains to forcefully extract information, or to predict if offenders might plan to commit future crimes.

But the secretary-general of the United Nations warned on Thursday for the first time that neurotechnologies are advancing so rapidly that governments’ ability to access and manipulate people’s brains could one day pose a threat to fundamental human rights.

The abuse of future technologies, Secretary-General António Guterres warned, could lead to arbitrary detentions, the alteration of people’s mental states and infringements on privacy.

“Neurotechnology, including new and emerging forms, raises profound human rights challenges when applied to the administration of justice,” the secretary-general wrote. “Its expansion beyond clinical settings into investigative, judicial and correctional contexts introduces significant risks, alongside potential benefits.”

To address such threats, the report lists a number of recommendations, including establishing regulations consistent with international law, recognizing thoughts as “highly sensitive personal data” and requiring explicit consent for the use of neurotechnology in criminal justice settings.

Human rights officials said the document was an important step toward raising global awareness of the issue and that it could help countries develop laws to prevent the abuse of such technology.

“This gives states an opportunity to establish clear rules to regulate the use of neurotechnology, based on human rights, before they become routine in investigations, courts and prisons,” said Jeremy Laurence, a spokesman for the U.N. Human Rights Office.

The report, some rights activists said, broadens the traditional understanding of freedom of thought, which has largely focused on freedom of expression, to include keeping one’s innermost ideas private.

“It’s no longer just about the classical ways through which freedom of thought is evoked,” said Marcello Ienca, a professor of ethics and neuroscience at the Technical University of Munich.

The U.N.’s interest comes amid a growing global push to protect brain data. Chile in 2012 enshrined protections for brain activity in its constitution. And several states, including California, Colorado and Montana, have passed laws protecting neural data. Similar measures have been proposed in Argentina, Brazil, Colombia and Mexico.

But while some countries are working to protect citizens’ neural data, others are already attempting to access it.

In India, the police have for two decades used a technology called Brain Electrical Oscillation Signature — or BEOS — to determine whether a suspect may have been involved in a crime.

The scientific basis for this technology, which reads brain waves, is scant. Results from BEOS tests are inadmissible as evidence in Indian courts, but the technology has been applied in hundreds of high-stakes cases, including those of murder, rape and terrorism.

BEOS has not been validated by the international scientific community. And a committee established by the Indian government to review BEOS concluded in 2008 that it was “sub-optimal.”

Not all neurotechnologies are being developed as tools of the state. Many have been brought to the consumer market as wearable health and wellness gadgets that can help users monitor their stress, sleep and focus.

But those too, experts warned, are subject to few regulations.

The Neurorights Foundation analyzed the privacy policies of 30 consumer neurotechnology companies in 2024 and found that most did not have limits on how they used customers’ brain data. More than half of those companies, the foundation said, explicitly allowed user data to be shared with third parties.

Neurotechnologies have also become powerful clinical tools for patients who have suffered severe brain or spinal cord injuries. Brain-computer interfaces have helped paralyzed patients to write sentences by imagining handwriting, as well as to move robotic limbs and to play chess online just by thinking.

item.title: The Man City Scandal Is About More Than Football
item.description:
Manchester City first came to my attention after we moved from Berlin to Cardiff and my then-8-year-old son, an avid football fan, declared that Man City was now his team. It was 2024, and the club had just won its fourth consecutive Premier League title — unheard of. That was clearly enough for my Welsh son to set aside any misgivings he might have had about supporting an English club.

Those titles don’t look so shiny now. Last month, an independent commission found Man City had broken more than 100 of the league’s financial rules. It said the team, whose majority owner is Sheikh Mansour bin Zayed Al Nahyan, the vice president of the United Arab Emirates, spent hundreds of millions of pounds it wasn’t allowed to spend, on players it could never have otherwise afforded. (Man City is appealing the ruling.)

I spoke to my colleague Tariq Panja, our global sports correspondent, about the biggest financial scandal in football history.

So Tariq, let’s talk about the scandal at Man City. Full disclosure: My 10-year-old is a Man City fan.

He’s not the only one! Kids love a winning team, and this generation of kids only know Man City as a winning team. But historically this was Manchester’s second team. It really wasn’t known for any great success — until Sept. 1, 2008. That’s the day Sheikh Mansour bought the club.

Why did Sheikh Mansour want to own Man City — or any football club for that matter?

Well, it is in the Premier League, which is the biggest league in the world. Millions of people watch it every year. It’s Britain’s biggest soft power export, bar none. For people wanting to burnish their personal image or their country’s image, it’s the epitome of sporting greatness. It gives you immediate name recognition. It’s a shortcut to respectability.

But it also brings scrutiny. Because if he didn’t own Man City, few in Britain would know who Sheikh Mansour is.

And of course that scrutiny has now come back to bite him. So tell me, someone who doesn’t watch the Premier League, what happened?

It’s massive. It’s the biggest financial cheating scandal in the history of football. To put it simply, they cooked the books in order to spend money they weren’t allowed to spend on an array of world-class talent.

You can only spend what you earn. There are three buckets of income for football teams: TV rights, stadium tickets and sponsorship. The first two, you can’t really manipulate. The third one is, according to a panel of arbitrators, the one that they really went to town on.

How so?

They signed a bunch of sham contracts with sponsors — U.A.E.-owned companies, like Etihad Airways. But those companies paid for a tiny fraction of that sponsorship. The rest of it came from Sheikh Mansour’s company, which was padding those numbers to an enormous degree. Of the roughly 950 million pounds of supposed sponsorship money Man City was claiming, only 120 million or so actually came from sponsors.

And all that money allowed it to buy players it would otherwise not have been able to afford?

Exactly. It allowed City to buy one of the best managers, Pep Guardiola, and some of the best players — Kevin De Bruyne, David Silva, Sergio Aguero — and pay them some of the biggest wages in the business. They’ve won eight Premier League titles under Sheikh Mansour’s ownership.

So who was hurt by this?

Where to start? Man City took the best players from so many rival teams over the years. From its traditional rival, Manchester United, from Arsenal, but also from mid-ranking teams like Aston Villa, who for three summers during this period had their best player taken by Man City. It changed the trajectory of lives, of careers, of teams for a decade.

And then there is the financial damage. A place in the Champions League is worth tens of millions of euros a year. So the team that didn’t make the Champions League — because Man City took a spot that should have gone to them — potentially lost huge amounts of revenue, sponsorship and the like.

OK, let’s talk about the politics of this. Is there any potential political cost for Britain in punishing a major Gulf investor?

The politics of this are very tricky. The U.A.E., which is a British ally, now stands accused of corrupting Britain’s biggest cultural export to the world. Bloomberg reported that Emirati officials have warned that a harsh punishment could have consequences for future investments in Britain.

And it’s created a headache for the prime minister, Andy Burnham. Remember, he was mayor of Greater Manchester until recently. He knows these people very well. The huge amount of investment his city attracted over the last decade? Some of that can be linked to Abu Dhabi. So now there is also scrutiny on Burnham and what kind of relationship he had with them.

How do Man City fans feel about all this?

Well, for the past decade, they just rallied around their club. Because this is a core part of their identity. They’re suddenly successful as a club, and here the world is telling them, “You’re cheating.”

But I would say that since the verdict, there has been a change in tone. There are still the zealots who refuse to think it’s anything but a conspiracy. But some are now saying, “Guys, we might have been wrong.” Some are really sad that it’s happened. Some are angry their club was used for this.

What will happen to Man City now?

Everything is on the table because we haven’t seen a scandal like this in the history of the Premier League. It could be relegated — demoted down a division or two. It could be banned from buying talent. Or given a massive penalty on points. Or charged a financial penalty. But some people are calling for it to be thrown out of the league altogether. That would be the most extreme punishment.

The West African staple lends color and umami to rich broths, lovingly slicks bitter greens and adds a floral yet smoky essence to anything in its path. (Don’t confuse it with refined palm oil, a tasteless, odorless ingredient used in cosmetics and commercial food production.)

Read conversations with four women across the diaspora about an oil that is a conduit to African food culture.

Adichie’s characters and her stories explore the sometimes fraught nature of being Nigerian, through tales of migration in “Americanah,” and civil war in “Half of a Yellow Sun.” “I think that America made it possible for me to write, which is my life’s vocation,” she told The Times from her home in Maryland. “But Nigeria gave me everything I needed to be able to write.”

Less than a year ago, while her family was spending the holidays in Lagos, Adichie’s 21-month-old son, Nkanu, died. The tragedy was met with an outpouring of grief and frustration, as many Nigerians shared their own negative experiences with the country’s health care system. As close readers of this newsletter know, I live in Wales. I’ve used this space before to share stories about what it’s like to live in a small, proud place. The sense of community. The pleasantly short commutes. The two degrees of separation that mean someone who’s either related to my husband or went to school with him can sort me out with tickets to, well, pretty much anything.

Which is how last night I found myself at the Welsh Music Awards. Finally, the Welsh Music Inspiration Award went to Mary Hopkin, an absolute legend. Paul McCartney produced her. She sang backing vocals for David Bowie. Her most famous song is both a masterpiece and a great way to finish the week: “Those Were the Days.”

item.title: Spain’s Protesters See ‘Madness’ of Rising Rent and a ‘Martyr’ in Maricarmen
item.description:
Thousands of people marched in Madrid on Thursday in memory of María del Carmen Abascal, the 87-year-old whose dramatic eviction two weeks ago shook the country and prompted Spain’s left-wing prime minister to call snap elections over a housing crisis.

Before her death on Wednesday, Ms. Abascal, popularly known as Maricarmen, became a symbol of the housing crisis. Only about 20 percent of Spaniards have to rent their homes, but that share has increased in recent years as homeownership — deeply ingrained in Spain’s culture — slides further out of reach.

Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez has portrayed his decision to hold elections as a chance for his left-wing bloc to get a majority in Parliament that would tackle the housing crisis. But it remains far from clear whether the issue will sway enough voters, as conservative and far-right parties frame the election as a referendum on Mr. Sánchez himself.

And as the parties wrangle, many Spaniards are staying in the streets, saying they feel crushed by the problems of rising rent and stagnant wages.

Nationally, rents have risen 87 percent since 2015, while salaries have climbed only 28 percent, according to an analysis by the newspaper El País. As a result, many young Spaniards stay in their parents’ homes well into their 30s. Newly arrived migrants pack into small apartments with other families. And many longtime residents are forced to leave their neighborhoods as their rents jump.

I spoke with dozens of protesters on Thursday evening about why they had joined the march, their own housing situations and what Ms. Abascal meant to them.

In Madrid’s Puerta del Sol, a central plaza of the capital and the origin of Thursday’s march, hundreds of tents have sprung up since Ms. Abascal’s eviction.

Among the protesters there was Alejandra Osés, a 22-year-old creative writing graduate student who has camped out for 10 days. “It’s becoming very difficult to find a place to live,” she said. “Maricarmen was the last straw.”

Ms. Osés shares an apartment in Madrid that rents for €1,500 a month, or about $1,680. While apartment hunting, she encountered rooms “without windows, places with barely any space, where you had to squeeze past a wardrobe to get into a room.”

After that struggle, she said, “the question is: How could I not be here?”

Beside her was Santiago Larraín, 22, a Chilean immigrant who studies acting and takes occasional jobs in cleaning and hospitality. He shares a two-bedroom apartment outside Madrid with his mother, who works as a cleaner, and two siblings. They pay roughly $1,345 a month.

“I’m here today because I have a mother,” he said. “And I think about how my mother could be Maricarmen, because we’re also going to be forced out of our apartment.”

Finding housing in Spain, he said, is a “bingo game of compassion and pity” with tenants left at the whims of the market.

A few hundred meters away, near Madrid’s landmark Bear and Strawberry Tree statue, hundreds of demonstrators had gathered, including Fernando Manjón, 29, and João Didelet, 27.

“Maricarmen has become something of a martyr for this social cause,” said Mr. Manjón, who earns $1,900 a month working for a nonprofit and shares an apartment that rents for $1,400 a month. When his landlord recently tried to raise his rent, he successfully challenged the increase.

“Life is already difficult,” he said. “I mean, paying rent, living in Madrid and then wanting to save for other things — it just gets harder and harder.”

Mr. Didelet, from Portugal, pays $460 for a room in a shared apartment, an amount many others consider cheap. But he cannot imagine being able to afford a place of his own.

“That’s a dream I can’t even contemplate,” he said.

Alfonso Lechón, 72, a retired teacher, looked over an altar the tenants’ union had set up beside a photograph of Maricarmen.

Mr. Lechón has owned his apartment in San Blas, a working-class neighborhood on Madrid’s outskirts, since 1982. He also inherited a small property by the beach and receives a decent pension.

“Personally, I have nothing to complain about,” he said. “But what I see around me is complicated.”

His neighborhood has changed dramatically, he said. In his apartment complex, built by a taxi drivers’ cooperative, rents have nearly doubled in recent years, from $670 or $780 a month to more than $1,345.

“The madness has reached us there, too,” he said.

He said he also worries about his son, who rents an apartment in Galicia, and his grandson.

“I think we need to make housing a right, just like education and health care,” he said.

Carlos Sánchez, 36, an architect, said he had joined the demonstration because he was deeply moved by Ms. Abascal’s death.

“Maricarmen isn’t the only one. There are many people in Spain who are losing their homes,” he said.

Mr. Sánchez shares an apartment with a roommate in Lavapiés, a neighborhood popular with tourists. They pay $900 a month, far below the $1,345 he estimates the apartment would fetch on the market.

He considers himself lucky to have a landlord who raises the rent only in line with inflation. “It sounds like I’m standing here describing the world’s greatest landlord,” he said, “when really he’s just the kind of landlord every landlord should be.”

As an architect, he has struggled with poorly paid jobs and internships. Rising rents and stagnant wages, he said, had left him with little hope for the future.

“It just eats up your salary,” he said of high rents. “You’re left with nothing.”

item.title: Malaysia Welcomes Myanmar’s Autocrat
item.description:
Over the past few months, he has traveled to Russia, China, India, Belarus, Cambodia, Vietnam, Thailand and Laos. Now, the leader of one of the world’s most repressive governments, U Min Aung Hlaing of Myanmar, is being feted by Malaysia, where he met on Thursday with Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim.

The summit, in which the two sides discussed the repatriation of Myanmar asylum-seekers in Malaysia and investment opportunities in a war-torn Myanmar, was the latest sign of a remarkable makeover for Mr. Min Aung Hlaing. Five years ago, he presided over a military coup that plunged Myanmar into full-blown civil war and made the Southeast Asian nation a global outcast.

But after trading his military uniform for civilian clothes earlier this year, the onetime junta leader has been basking in international recognition. In public remarks on Thursday, Mr. Anwar declined to utter a single critical word about the reign of terror unleashed under Mr. Min Aung Hlaing’s rule.

“Now we have had excellent relations for a long time, but of course, recent developments have somewhat blocked that sort of progress, so I think our interest is, of course, to enhance this collaboration,” Mr. Anwar said, in a delicate description of the coup and its deadly aftermath.

Since taking the presidential post, Mr. Min Aung Hlaing has traveled to five countries in the Association of Southeast Asian Nations, or ASEAN. But he is still officially banned from attending its summits, an international affirmation that he craves, Myanmar observers say.

Mr. Anwar gave a wink-wink acknowledgment of the Myanmar leader’s efforts to work himself back into ASEAN’s good graces.

“You will continue your policy to engage with all parties to avoid further escalation of violence, and of course, I welcome that and convey it to my colleagues not only here but also in ASEAN,” Mr. Anwar said.

In April, Mr. Min Aung Hlaing became president, following his retirement as army chief and a set of stage-managed elections that the military’s proxy party contested virtually unopposed. Since then, the military’s attacks on civilian nationwide have not abated. A.C.L.E.D., a conflict monitoring group, says that Myanmar is one of the most dangerous places on earth, the severity of its conflict outranked only by that in the Palestinian territories. Last week, at least 50 people were killed in a military airstrike on a market in western Myanmar.

The two-day visit to Malaysia marked a rare foray by Mr. Min Aung Hlaing, one of the world’s leading jailers of political prisoners, to a nation that regularly holds unfettered elections. Mr. Anwar himself spent nearly 11 years in prison for what are widely regarded as politically motivated convictions.

On Thursday, a “cooperation dialogue” after the two leaders’ 40-minute tête-à-tête was dominated by business discussions. Among those attending on the Malaysian side were the trade minister and the central bank head, as well as top figures representing the palm oil industry, a telecommunications conglomerate, private banks and the state-owned oil and natural gas company. Mr. Anwar said that year-on-year trade with Myanmar had increased more than 140 percent.

After the coup, major democracies placed financial sanctions on members of Myanmar’s military leadership, as well as on the cronies propping up the regime. But on Thursday, the Myanmar delegation in Putrajaya, the Malaysian administrative capital, was studded with businessmen and generals-turned-cabinet ministers who are the subjects of asset freezes, travel bans and other financial restrictions imposed by Western nations.

Myanmar’s economy, once buoyed by foreign investment during a brief reform period, has contracted sharply since the military takeover, a downturn that Mr. Min Aung Hlaing has blamed on foreign sanctions and rebel incursions. More than two-thirds of Myanmar’s population is impoverished or in danger of falling into poverty, according to a new report from the United Nations Development Program.

Mr. Anwar’s decision to welcome the Myanmar leader comes amid growing xenophobia toward migrants in Malaysia, which prompted his plan to deport people from Myanmar back home. On Thursday, he praised Mr. Min Aung Hlaing for his “candid manner and willingness to collaborate” on the mass repatriation.

“Very few, hardly any country, in my experience, are willing to accept this repatriation in a large, in large number, at their own expense, as you have shown in Myanmar,” Mr. Anwar said.

The first batch of about 1,470 people left Malaysia on a Myanmar Navy ship a day after the airstrike killed more than 50 people in the country’s western Rakhine State. Much of Rakhine is now in the hands of a rebel militia. The Myanmar government minister for Rakhine was part of the Malaysia delegation.

Among the first deportees was Ko Min Nyan Tun, who said that he had to sign a document absolving Malaysia of legal responsibility if the ship back faced any difficulties. The journey itself was comfortable, he said, with plentiful food and karaoke breaks, although his family was made to pay the Myanmar Navy for these luxuries. His dread grew when he returned to Myanmar, he said, because he was given signals that he would likely be drafted into the military.

Fear of conscription has led at least a million young people to flee Myanmar since the coup. More than half the country is now in the hands of armed rebel groups, and the military has made up for a soldier shortfall by drafting men to the age of 35 and women to 27.

Mr. Min Nyan Tun, 34, said he has now been deported three times from Malaysia. But he said he would head back there again, somehow.

“If I had to choose between being arrested again in Malaysia and being sent to the front line, I would choose going back to Malaysia,” he said. “I can’t go to the front line and give my life for the military regime.”

Hundreds of thousands of people from Myanmar are believed to be working menial jobs in Malaysia without documentation. Around 215,000 refugees or asylum seekers from Myanmar are registered in Malaysia with the United Nations refugee agency.

Before the coup, Malaysia, a Muslim-majority nation, absorbed a population of Rohingya, a Muslim ethnicity from Myanmar that has long suffered repression. Effectively stateless, waves of Rohingya were violently expelled from their homeland nearly a decade ago, an exodus that ranks as one of the fastest refugee outflows in recent history. A genocide case against Myanmar is underway at the International Court of Justice at The Hague, with a ruling expected in the coming months.

After the first repatriations on Sept. 30, Mr. Anwar said that no Rohingya had been sent to Myanmar. But the prime minister also said last month that he wants to expel the entire population of Myanmar refugees and asylum seekers in Malaysia. The majority of them are Rohingya. Complicating matters, Mr. Min Aung Hlaing said on Thursday that Myanmar would only repatriate “those confirmed as Myanmar citizens.” His government does not consider Rohingya to be from Myanmar.

“The idea that the refugee flow will somehow end after a meeting between Anwar and Min Aung Hlaing is ignorance,” said Charles Santiago, the Malaysian co-chair of ASEAN Parliamentarians for Human Rights. “The flow will end when the violence ends.”

Mr. Min Aung Hlaing’s visit to Malaysia was capped by a state luncheon in which the guests feasted on lamb with mint and black pepper sauces, jumbo prawns in buttermilk and a cheese and passion fruit pudding, among other delights.

One in three people in Myanmar, the U.N. says, now does not have enough to eat.

item.title: Hacker Used Chinese-Developed A.I. Tool to Target South Korean Banks, CrowdStrike Says
item.description:
The cybersecurity firm CrowdStrike said Wednesday that a recent string of cyberattacks against banks in South Korea may have been carried out by a hacker using Chinese and American artificial intelligence tools.

CrowdStrike said the attacker had used ARTEX, a recently released open source tool developed in China, and A.I. tools including Anthropic’s Claude Code in a “targeted campaign” against South Korean financial organizations between September and October. It found internet addresses and files from the tools using publicly accessible data, the firm said.

“While this activity has not been attributed to a named adversary, the threat actor is likely a Chinese speaker and financially motivated,” the company said in a report published Wednesday. It added that it had “moderate confidence” in its assessment, which it said was based on the hacker’s use of ARTEX and prompts written in Chinese.

The report comes as countries around the world are grappling with the increasing abilities of A.I. agents, raising alarm about the pace of their development and questioning whether adequate safeguards are in place for the fast-evolving technology.

In South Korea, anxiety surrounding A.I. has sent the country’s stock market on a roller-coaster ride. The nation’s benchmark Kospi index, which doubled in the first half of this year, fell quickly during the summer over concerns about the technology.

Those anxieties have risen in the past several weeks as details emerged about hacking attacks on different South Korean banks, in which the personal credit information of thousands of customers was leaked.

Earlier this week, South Korean officials said they were investigating the breaches, but provided little information about who was behind them. President Lee Jae Myung said that “signs have emerged” that A.I. models had been used in some of the cyberattacks, “causing considerable public concern and anxiety.”

The South Korean police said it had no comment on the CrowdStrike report while its investigation was underway.

CrowdStrike said in its report on Wednesday that the possible hacker its researchers tracked had on one occasion asked Claude where people go to sell stolen Korean data.

Another time, the user asked Claude to create a “security researcher résumé” and provided details such as the name “YY,” along with a phone number, age, university and the name of a Chinese city. When The New York Times called the phone number on Thursday, a man picked up the phone, speaking Chinese and using obscenities, and said he was not “YY.”

CrowdStrike said that the résumé information, including the phone number, most likely belonged to the user, but it could not say so definitively.

Despite apprehensions over the use of A.I., South Korea has largely embraced the technology and benefited from the global boom. Its monthly semiconductor exports hit a record-breaking $60.3 billion in September, more than triple compared to the same period last year, according to the government. And the nation’s gross domestic product has gone up because of it.

Choe Sang-Hun contributed reporting.

item.title: Inside the Russian Warehouses Bombarded by Ukraine
item.description:
It was two days before the start of school, and David Zelensky, 16, was earning some final summer cash at an e-commerce warehouse in the Russian city of Belgorod.

The oldest of nine children, David had landed the job a few weeks earlier at the online retailer Ozon, an upgrade from his former gig delivering food. He settled in for an evening shift on Aug. 30 that would put him closer to his dream of buying a motorcycle.

Then came the Ukrainian missiles.

First, the city air raid sirens wailed. Next, an explosion from what seemed to be the interception of a rocket rang out.

As workers ran across the warehouse floor toward a shelter, a missile slammed into the building. The lights went dark. Walls and metal shelves crashed down on a group of high school and college students as a fireball engulfed part of the facility.

David, who communicated with fellow workers by writing on a phone because he was deaf and unable to speak, was killed. A 21-year-old college student also died, and a 16-year-old boy was critically injured.

“It was hard to process the fact that, just moments ago, I had seen people alive and well, and then suddenly they were gone,” said another student who was injured at the warehouse.

The student was one of more than a dozen e-commerce workers interviewed by The New York Times from warehouses across Russia. They described how incoming drones, hourslong middle-of-the-night evacuations and fears of injury or death had become the new norm at work.

Some of the workers spoke on the condition of anonymity out of fear of being fired. In other cases, The Times is withholding their identity for security reasons.

The events in Belgorod illustrate the danger that civilian employees at Russia’s two e-commerce giants, Ozon and Wildberries, are facing as Ukraine has transformed the companies into a new front in the war.

For years, Moscow’s invasion has forced Ukrainians to make life-or-death decisions every day. Now, more Russians are having to do the same, as Kyiv’s missiles and drones shatter the illusion of normalcy carefully conjured by President Vladimir V. Putin.

“Personally, to be honest, I can’t believe it,” said a 19-year-old employee at a Wildberries warehouse outside Moscow.

The employee encountered his first drone strike at the facility last month. “It’s an absolute nightmare,” he said.

Ukraine has argued that the warehouses are legitimate targets because the retailers sell components that can be used to fix Russian military drones and protective equipment for Russian soldiers.

Russian officials and the head of Wildberries, Tatyana Kim, have dismissed the rationale, calling the strikes “terrorist attacks” against civilians. Wildberries and Ozon did not respond to requests for comment.

The toll of the Ukrainian attacks on Russian warehouses is vastly exceeded by the civilian suffering that Russia is causing in Ukraine.

Two months of frequent strikes on Wildberries and Ozon facilities killed 12 people and injured 135 through Sept. 11, according to the Conflict Intelligence Team, an open-source research group tracking wartime civilian casualties.

By comparison, Russia killed more Ukrainians in a single attack on a shopping mall in the Ukrainian city of Kryvyi Rih on Aug. 21. In that strike, 16 people died and another 136 were injured, according to the research group. Moscow has also attacked large numbers of Ukrainian warehouses.

Broadly, the Conflict Intelligence Team figures show that 66 percent of reported civilian deaths in the war this year have taken place in Ukraine, compared with 19 percent in Russian-occupied parts of Ukraine and 15 percent in Russia itself.

Still, for many employees at the Russian warehouses, the regular threat of attack has come as a shock.

At a Wildberries warehouse near Domodedovo Airport in the Moscow region, workers ran out of the facility one morning at 3 a.m. as drones descended on the area. They took cover under the bridge of a nearby highway, waiting four hours until after the sun came up to return, one worker recalled.

Outside Moscow, at a Wildberries warehouse in Novoselki, workers repeatedly flee into the woods during evacuations. They wonder whether they will freeze this coming winter when they have to drop everything and leave on cold days.

A worker at that warehouse recalled taking a cigarette break on a recent day and watching as a Ukrainian drone exploded in the parking lot 50 yards away, without any siren or alarm going off.

“When one actually lands right next to you — when you can even hear the metal ball bearings raining down from the sky — that’s when the real fear kicks in,” the worker said, noting that some employees now flee calmly, while newer hires run in panic.

A few of the warehouse workers who spoke to The Times decided to quit, citing safety concerns. But the vast majority have stayed on the job, noting that the work pays better and is more flexible than other options.

Wildberries workers say they can show up and leave whenever they want, including in the middle of the night, and work for as many hours as they choose. Workers also receive most of their pay immediately. Some say they can earn as much as $2,900 a month, well over double the average monthly pay in Russia, though earnings vary based on the volume of work.

As a result, many have adapted to the fraught new reality.

One worker at a Wildberries warehouse in Yekaterinburg recalled how even after a drone slammed into the parking lot and burned about 50 cars belonging to employees, workers kept showing up. They simply parked their cars next to the burned-out vehicles.

Another worker who was employed at a Wildberries warehouse in the Tula region described how, after his workplace was blown up, he started traveling two and a half hours a day to work at a different Wildberries warehouse, in the Moscow region. He said he faced hostility there from people worried that the influx of labor would reduce wages and work.

In recent weeks, the Russian authorities have pressed companies to erect defenses, with nets and scaffolding going up around installations to blunt the impact of drone attacks.

In Yekaterinburg, the Wildberries warehouse put water barrels on the roof to suppress fires, erected nets and fencing, and installed an exhaust system to clear smoke rapidly, the worker there said.

On the evening of the attack at the Ozon warehouse in Belgorod, where David worked, supervisors gathered the staff for a five-minute safety briefing.

David had a shift from 5 p.m. to 10 p.m. at the placement station, where workers load incoming packages into bins for sorting, according to another worker who saw him that day.

What exactly transpired in David’s final minutes is unclear.

While he most likely could not have heard the siren go off or the initial blast from the intercepted missile, he could have received other alerts. Hand-held inventory scanners used by workers would flash warnings during attacks, sometimes with a delay, one worker said. David may also have been warned by others or may have seen co-workers running.

Regardless, there was very little time.

In drone attacks, people often have time to take cover. But missiles arrive quickly, and one worker said that no one had expected the Ukrainians to use missiles on the comparatively small Ozon warehouse.

Ozon has since barred minors from working at its warehouses in some regions, according to Russian news outlets. The company also offered compensation to the Belgorod workers, with higher sums for those with more serious injuries, employees said.

Not long after the strike, David’s family gathered for a funeral.

His father, also born deaf and nonspeaking, and his mother, born with a hearing impairment, were there, his aunt, Anna Polushkina, told The Times. So were four of his eight siblings, all of whom are also either deaf or hearing-impaired, she said. While the family shared the same surname as President Volodymyr Zelensky of Ukraine, there was no indication that they were related, Ms. Polushkina said.

At the funeral, the attendees hugged and cried. His friends placed a small motorcycle atop a display of roses and carnations at the grave. There were wafer cakes, a nod to his love of sweets.

David’s school, a special educational institution for children with disabilities, put out a statement calling his death an irreparable loss. The regional sports ministry said that he had shown great promise as a player on a basketball team for the hearing impaired.

“He dreamed about a motorcycle,” Ms. Polushkina said. “He really loved to ride.”

“As for an attack,” she said, “we never imagined anything like this.”

Alina Lobzina contributed reporting.

item.title: South Korea Recalls Envoy From Ukraine in Dispute Over North Korean POWs
item.description:
South Korea announced on Thursday that it will recall its ambassador to Ukraine, deepening a diplomatic rift sparked last month when President Volodymyr Zelensky of Ukraine revealed his government had sent two North Korean prisoners of war to Seoul.

The government of President Lee Jae Myung of South Korea was caught off guard by the disclosure of the defections, which Mr. Zelensky made during a speech at the United Nations General Assembly. The two North Koreans were among the thousands from their country who had been fighting for Russia in its war against Ukraine.

Mr. Lee, whose domestic critics have accused him of trying to keep the move secret to protect efforts to improve ties with Pyongyang, immediately expressed displeasure.

He said that Seoul and Kyiv had mutually agreed to keep the soldiers’ defections confidential to help ensure their safety, along with that of their families in North Korea. He accused Kyiv of breaking a bilateral confidentiality agreement, calling the move “regrettable.” Kyiv has said that no agreement existed.

A diplomatic tit-for-tat ensued. In interviews published by Ukrainian media outlets last week, the country’s foreign minister, Andrii Sybiha, sought to defuse the situation, calling it a “diplomatic misunderstanding.” The characterization only fueled Mr. Lee’s frustration.

“When the South Korean president expressed regret with the utmost courtesy, they claimed there was no agreement, making the head of state of another country out to be a liar,” Mr. Lee said. “If they continue to refuse to acknowledge the facts and issue a public apology, we will take additional measures.”

Testifying before the National Assembly on Tuesday, the South Korean foreign minister, Cho Hyun, said the response South Korea had received from Mr. Sybiha fell short of the apology it had demanded. Mr. Cho warned of a “resolute step.”

He didn’t elaborate. But on Thursday, South Korea followed through on its warning by recalling its ambassador to Ukraine, Park Ki-chang.

“The government hopes for an amicable resolution to the pending issue between the two countries and will continue consultations with the Ukrainian side,” the South Korean Foreign Ministry said in an official statement.

Recalling an ambassador represents a severe diplomatic expression of discontent. South Korea last took such action in 2008, when it summoned home its ambassador to Japan over a territorial dispute.

The two North Korean soldiers were captured in January of last year while fighting in the Kursk region of Russia. Seoul and Kyiv subsequently engaged in secret negotiations over the fate of the two men, who expressed a desire to defect to South Korea. Under its Constitution, South Korea recognizes all North Koreans as its citizens and maintains a legal obligation to accept defectors and refugees from the North.

Following Mr. Zelensky’s disclosure, South Korean lawmakers confirmed the soldiers had arrived in Seoul in the middle of last month.

South Korea has consistently denounced Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, providing Kyiv with medical supplies, financial aid, and nonlethal military equipment like helmets and demining gear. Mr. Zelensky has repeatedly urged Seoul to do more, asking for missiles and other South Korean weapons, but South Korea has declined, citing its longstanding policy against supplying lethal weapons to countries at war.

The kingdom has been left reeling, with the Saudi authorities saying on Wednesday that Houthi strikes on airports in Riyadh and Abha, a city in the south of the country, had killed three people and injured dozens more.

The attacks are the deadliest on Saudi Arabia since the war with the Houthis reignited in recent weeks and threaten to widen a conflict that has entangled multiple countries and strained energy markets. Oil prices rose sharply on Thursday, with Brent crude, the global benchmark, up more than 5 percent.

The instability snarled air traffic, with around one in four departures from Saudi airports and dozens of inbound flights canceled, according to data from the aviation analytics firm Cirium. The Lufthansa Group suspended flights to Riyadh up to Oct. 16, the company said. And Air India’s flights to the Saudi capital were also paused, according to the Indian Embassy there.

The Saudi authorities did not respond to questions on the Houthis’ claims.

The New York Times has verified two videos circulating on social media that showed a thick plume of black smoke billowing over Riyadh’s airport, which has announced dozens of flight cancellations.

The targeting of Riyadh has raised pressure on Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, the kingdom’s de facto leader, to resolve the escalating conflict as the fighting threatens his plans to turn the country into a business and tourism hub. Riyadh is set to host several international events in the coming weeks, including an annual investment summit hosted by Prince Mohammed that is typically attended by world leaders, billionaires and top global executives.

Saudi Arabia announced a new bombing campaign in Yemen this week against the Houthis, who have vowed to fight back by hitting airports and energy infrastructure.

Prince Mohammed has also sought to secure greater military support from allies, including the United States, which is providing significant assistance to the kingdom’s bombing campaign.

The fighting could entangle more parties, after Pakistan and Turkey this week activated a defense pact to provide military support to Saudi Arabia. A senior Pakistani military official, who spoke on the condition of anonymity to discuss operational matters, said on Wednesday that Pakistani fighter jets were being used in strikes against the Houthis.

It was unclear if foreign military intervention would temper attacks by the Houthis, who have survived years of bombing campaigns and have calculated that they can inflict greater pain on Saudi Arabia than the kingdom can on them.

A Times reporter in Riyadh heard several blasts in quick succession on Thursday morning. Two residents, who spoke on condition of anonymity, said workers at an office tower in the city had been told to evacuate. In recent days, the Saudi authorities have told residents not to share information related to missile and drone attacks, warning them of legal consequences.

The Houthis say that their attacks in Saudi Arabia are retaliation for attacks in Yemen.

The conflict in Yemen is being fought on multiple fronts. The internationally recognized government of Yemen, backed by Saudi warplanes, began a counteroffensive this week to retake strategically important territory along the Red Sea from the Houthis. The militia seized parts of the coast last month in a move that gave it greater control over the Bab al-Mandab Strait, a critical global trade route.

The Houthis say they have made gains in the inland city of Taiz, a government stronghold.

A Yemeni government army officer in Taiz said that Houthi forces had effectively encircled the city and that residents were running out of gas and food supplies. He spoke on condition of anonymity as he was not authorized to speak to the media.

A spokesman for the Saudi-led military coalition, Maj. Gen. Turki al-Maliki, said overnight that it had attacked dozens of Houthi military sites, including missile storage facilities and command centers, in retaliation for the airport strikes on Wednesday. The Houthis did not respond to that claim.

The latest round of fighting has plunged Saudi Arabia and the Houthis back into open conflict, and nearly 200,000 Yemenis have been displaced since September, when the fighting intensified, according to the United Nations.

In 2015, Saudi Arabia led a disastrous campaign against the Houthis in a bid to restore Yemen’s government, which had been driven out of the capital, Sanaa, by the militia.

The war led to hundreds of thousands of deaths and created one of the world’s worst humanitarian crises, until the two sides agreed to a tenuous truce in 2022.

Senator Chris Murphy, Democrat of Connecticut, who met with Prince Mohammed on Monday in Riyadh and publicly opposed the kingdom’s last campaign in Yemen, said that it was unclear what the kingdom’s long-term objectives are in its renewed military campaign.

“They want to win back the territory that they’ve lost, and I think the open question is whether they have clear goals beyond that,” Mr. Murphy told reporters. “I think history tells us that this military conflict, whoever starts it, is a disaster for the people of Yemen, for the region, and for the United States.”

Analysts said the attacks on Riyadh in recent days would make it more likely that the Saudi government would intensify its bombing campaign in Yemen.

“The latest attack just gives them more international support for any military operation they would do against the Houthis,” said Farea al-Muslimi, a Yemen specialist at Chatham House, a London-based research group.

President Trump has rebuffed Saudi government requests to direct American airstrikes. But more than 200 U.S. intelligence and military analysts are assisting the Saudi government in command centers inside the kingdom, helping to analyze and select targets in support of its Yemeni allies, according to one current and one former U.S. official, who spoke on the condition of anonymity to discuss operational matters. The United States is also providing aerial refueling for Saudi warplanes conducting defensive air patrols, they added.

Last month, Britain also promised to offer limited aerial refueling to Saudi warplanes for defensive purposes. It is unclear if that will extend to the new campaign. France said last month that it would send troops and other military assets to protect Saudi energy infrastructure on the Red Sea.

Saeed Al-Batati contributed reporting from al-Mukalla, Yemen, and Pranav Baskar contributed reporting from New York.

item.title: Margaret Papandreou, American-Born First Lady of Greece, Dies at 102
item.description:
Margaret Papandreou, who helped transform legal and social rights for Greek women in the 1980s as the American-born wife of Prime Minister Andreas Papandreou and who later supported feminist and socialist movements around the world, died on Sept. 18 at her home in Palaio Faliro, a seaside suburb of Athens. She was 102.

Her family announced the death.

Ms. Papandreou’s tireless organizing and her direct pipeline to power were credited with spurring fundamental shifts in Greece that included legalizing abortion and removing antiquated social codes, such as requiring a husband’s permission for a woman to start a business or travel abroad with their children.

“The women’s movement is a political movement,” she said at a United Nations conference on women in Nairobi, Kenya, in 1985. “It is a social revolution. It is about changes in society, changes that are global.”

After a bitter public divorce in 1989, she expanded her role in international efforts to promote women in politics and retained prominence in Greece as matriarch of the third generation in a left-leaning political dynasty. Her son George A. Papandreou (pronounced Pap-an-DREY-oo) served as prime minister from 2009 to 2011.

With an easy smile and Midwestern openness that confused and charmed Greeks, Ms. Papandreou set the foundation for her influence in women’s issues during the heady era after the collapse of a seven-year military junta in 1974.

The Papandreous had fled from the junta’s crackdowns on dissent and were back from a self-exile in northern Europe and Canada, where Ms. Papandreou wrote a memoir, “Nightmare in Athens” (1970), recounting the events as dictatorship began in 1967. With the return of democracy, her husband’s Panhellenic Socialist Movement, or Pasok, was surging in strength.

Ms. Papandreou, who was known as Margarita in Greece, borrowed from the party’s populist-style tactics. She traveled across cities and rural areas to meet with women to discuss their aspirations and concerns, which at the time included the age-old system of the bride’s family providing a dowry before marriage. (It wasn’t until 1952 that Greek women could vote in national elections.)

Her efforts coalesced around the Women’s Union of Greece, a group she founded in 1975 and led for eight years. Opposition came from many directions. The Greek Orthodox Church claimed that Ms. Papandreou was undermining cultural traditions. Right-wing newspapers painted her as an interloper and made note of her American-accented Greek.

But national elections in 1981 gave Pasok a landslide victory and made her husband prime minister. “We’ve had enough of being second-class citizens, always pushed to the margin,” Ms. Papandreou said to a crowd of female voters at a pre-election rally for the Greek actress, singer and political activist Melina Mercouri, who was her husband’s ally. Ms. Mercouri won a seat in Parliament and was named culture minister.

Using the clout of her first lady status, Ms. Papandreou lobbied Pasok members in Parliament to act quickly on legislation to dismantle the restrictions on women.

Her crowning moment came in 1983 with the passage of a sweeping law that effectively gave women equal status on domestic issues and ended any lingering male-permission rules. The reforms also abolished dowries, created divorce by mutual consent and made single mothers the legal guardians of their children. In another first, women no longer had to change their names after marriage.

In 1986, Greece legalized abortion, making it one of the last Western European countries to end widespread restrictions — although some countries, including Poland and Malta, still maintain strict abortion regulations.

In a statement from President Constantine Tassoulas of Greece after Ms. Papandreou’s death, he described her as a cornerstone for “the reform of family law, the breakthrough in social and political rights, and the modernization of women’s status in Greek society.”

Apart from her political achievements, Ms. Papandreou’s legacy was also intertwined with modern Greece’s most watched breakup drama.

In a spectacle that played out in the press, she endured humiliation and responded with scorn after her husband of nearly 40 years and father of her four adult children started a relationship with Dimitra Liani, an Olympic Airways flight attendant who was half his age.

By the late 1980s, Ms. Liani had become the de facto first lady. She appeared with the prime minister during visits by dignitaries and at international events. In 1988, Ms. Liani and the prime minister were photographed walking hand in hand on the grounds of Harefield Hospital outside London, where he underwent heart surgery. Ms. Papandreou refused to visit him.

At first, Ms. Papandreou said she would not agree to a divorce, but she signed the papers in June 1989. The next month, just after finishing his second term, Mr. Papandreou, then 70, and Ms. Liani married. He was back in office from 1993 to 1996, resigning months before his death.

During Ms. Papandreou’s marital ordeal, public sympathy largely flowed to her because of how the prime minister flaunted his extramarital relationship in public.

“I refuse to be the victim,” Ms. Papandreou told The New York Times in 1989. “I believe I will come out of this very strong. Maybe I’ll come out of it the stronger of the two.”

Margaret Esther Chant, the oldest of five sisters, was born in Oak Park, Ill., on Sept. 30, 1923, and raised in nearby Elmhurst, west of Chicago. Her mother, Hulda (Pfund) Chant, was a homemaker, and her father, Douglas Chant, was a car mechanic who lost his job during the Great Depression.

The family’s financial struggles left a deep imprint on Margaret’s views on social justice.

“It seemed to me that there was something very unjust about people having a lot of money while others had none,” she later told The Washington Post. “The principles of socialism appealed to me. They were human goals, health, education, a right to work.”

At the University of Minnesota, she received a bachelor’s degree in journalism in 1946 and a master’s degree in public health in 1950. During her postgraduate studies, she started a small public relations firm in Minneapolis and struck a side deal to help a local dentist write his autobiography in exchange for free dental care.

While in the waiting room at the dentist’s office in 1948, she met Andreas Papandreou, an associate professor of economics at her alma mater and the son of a former Greek prime minister, George Papandreou, one of the pro-Western power brokers as Greece descended into factional fighting after World War II.

“By the end of that evening, I was in love with him,” she recalled to The Minneapolis Star Tribune in 1996. He was married at the time, and she was later briefly married to Robert L. Hall, a doctoral student in sociology. After their divorces, they wed each other in 1951.

Mr. Papandreou became chairman of the economics department at the University of California, Berkeley, in 1955, but he harbored ambitions as political heir to his father, and the couple relocated to Athens in 1961.

Mr. Papandreou’s political rise was soon underway after his father regained the prime minister post in the mid-1960s, a period of political upheavals when military commanders began plotting the coup. Ms. Papandreou came to wider notice to the Greek public in the coup’s aftermath as the junta rounded up left-leaning political leaders, students, intellectuals and others, including her husband.

She aggressively campaigned for his release, enlisting prominent friends like the economist and former U.S. diplomat John Kenneth Galbraith. After Mr. Papandreou was freed in 1968, the family left the country and eventually settled in Canada.

From their self-exile, Ms. Papandreou and her husband were increasingly dismayed by U.S. aid to the junta, which was seen by Washington as an anti-communist bulwark despite the regime’s repression and human rights violations.

For decades after, Ms. Papandreou and her husband remained sharp critics of U.S. policies, calling for the removal of military bases in Greece and describing unfettered capitalism as “anti-feminist.”

“I don’t hate the people there, or even the government,” she told The Globe and Mail of Toronto in 1983. “I just think it’s on the wrong track, that it neglects the interests of poor and oppressed people. But it would be nonsense to deny my past, my culture.”

In addition to her son George A. Papandreou, survivors include two other sons, Andreas Papandreou and Nikos Papandreou, a member of the European Parliament; a daughter, Sofia Papandreou; six grandchildren; and a great-granddaughter.

In 2015, Ms. Papandreou published a second memoir, “Love and Power: A Midwestern First Lady.” In speeches and interviews, she recounted being asked whether she ever dreamed she would become the wife of Greece’s prime minister.

“No,” she liked to say. “I dreamed I would grow up to be the prime minister of Greece.”

item.title: Escalating Assaults on Ukrainian Cities Are Taking an Enormous Toll
item.description:
It was a devastating scene in a devastated city.

Under shredded netting meant to shield civilians from Russian drones, near residential buildings shattered by explosions, the charred metal skeleton of a commuter bus was all that was left on Thursday after another Russian strike in Kramatorsk in eastern Ukraine.

At least 30 people were killed, local officials said, the latest civilian casualties in Moscow’s unrelenting campaign to make Ukraine’s towns and cities unlivable.

As rescue workers in Kramatorsk were tending to the injured and gathering body parts from the street, President Volodymyr Zelensky was making his way to another Ukrainian city, Pryluky, where he implored the world to do more to counter Russian aggression.

He stood near the rubble of an apartment building destroyed by a Russian missile on Wednesday, killing 22 people, including five children. Entire families died in that strike.

Speaking in Pryluky, which was hit despite being about 200 miles from any combat zone, Mr. Zelensky said that Russia was seeking ways to expand its advantage in the skies and unleash more terror.

He warned that China was developing technology meant to compete with the Starlink satellite network and planned to share it with Russia. He called on the United States to allow Ukraine to use Starlink to target Russian missile and drone launch sites inside Russia.

The price of inaction, Mr. Zelensky said, was scenes like those in Pryluky, where he met with rescue workers and grieving families.

The Russian military has attacked civilian homes throughout the war. But the death toll is rising as Moscow fields an ever-growing supply of powerful precision weapons, stretching Ukraine’s air defenses with daily onslaughts.

The Kremlin has expanded its arsenal of newly developed jet-powered drones and increased the range of powerful guided bombs dropped from warplanes. Russia is also employing new communication tools that allow pilots to remotely guide munitions for precision strikes from hundreds of miles away.

Russia launched about 3,500 jet-powered drones against targets across Ukraine in September, compared with 350 in June, according to the Ukrainian Air Force. Ukraine is working furiously to develop interceptors that work against the jet-powered drones, which travel hundreds of miles per hour.

On Thursday morning, one of those jet drones smashed into a store in downtown Kyiv, the Ukrainian capital, killing three people and injuring 14 others, city officials said.

The store was hit a day after a large-scale bombardment on Wednesday killed at least 30 people across the country, including six in the capital.

Mr. Zelensky noted that the bombardment, which included the cruise missile strike on the apartment complex in Pryluky, coincided with President Vladimir V. Putin’s 74th birthday.

“This is the kind of ‘gift’ Putin gave himself for his birthday,” Mr. Zelensky said on Wednesday. “The killing of children, the killing of people.”

While drones and missiles pose the biggest threat across Ukraine, frontline cities like Kramatorsk, where the bus was struck, are being slowly destroyed by artillery and guided bombs that can pack hundreds of pounds of explosives.

In August, Russia dropped a record 8,700 guided bombs on military and civilian targets, according to the Ukrainian military. The only reliable defense against these bombs, which can hit targets more than 100 miles from where they are released, is to take out the warplanes that deliver them or destroy the warehouses where they are stored.

The epicenter of the fighting remains the eastern Donetsk region, where the majority of glide bomb strikes are recorded. Ukraine still controls around 20 percent of the territory, including Kramatorsk, Sloviansk and other cities that make up a belt of heavily fortified land.

Around 93,000 civilians remain in areas under Ukrainian control in Donetsk, including more than 4,200 children, according to local officials.

“The Russians are deliberately targeting civilians,” Vadym Filashkin, the head of the Donetsk regional military administration, said in a statement after the attack on the bus. “For them, a bus carrying passengers is an attractive target precisely because a single strike can kill as many people as possible.”

Nataliia Novosolova and Liubov Sholudko contributed reporting.

item.description:
China has begun operating a new air force base in Laos, marking another step in Beijing’s efforts to establish military footholds abroad and project power into Southeast Asia.

Satellite images released this week revealed that eight small military aircraft had arrived at the China-Laos Joint Logistics and Training Center, which officially opened late last month at Ban Keun, about 30 miles north of the Laotian capital, Vientiane.

The satellite images, first reported by Reuters, showed a 1.2-mile runway at Ban Keun that could be extended, opening the possibility that the facility could host bigger aircraft that need longer takeoffs and landings.

The base in Laos, a landlocked country between Vietnam and Thailand, could help the Chinese air force reach across the region, including countries with which Beijing has long-running territorial tensions over the South China Sea, some experts said.

China has the world’s second biggest military after the United States. The People’s Liberation Army has been expanding rapidly but has taken limited only steps to open bases in other countries: a naval facility in Cambodia and another naval support center in Djibouti, in East Africa.

“Ban Keun is significant because it appears to be China’s first openly acknowledged overseas military facility for air power,” said Ying Yu Lin, an associate professor at Tamkang University in Taipei who studies China’s military. The new facility “sits in the center of the Indochinese peninsula, and could enable the Chinese Communist Party to easily project air power across surrounding areas.”

But for now at least, the Chinese air force presence at Ban Keun is too small and isolated to have tangible military consequences, said Drew Thompson, a former Pentagon official.

“Laos is landlocked, so a base there doesn’t give the Lao or Chinese air force unfettered access to the Indian Ocean or Gulf of Thailand,” said Mr. Thompson, who is now a senior fellow at the S. Rajaratnam School of International Studies at Nanyang Technological University in Singapore. “The threat of a joint Lao-China air force base is primarily political rather than military because it was established without consultation” with Laos’ neighbors.

The eight aircraft at Ban Keun were possibly K-8 jets, also called Hongdu JL-8, a light two-seater built by China and Pakistan that is mostly used for training, said Professor Lin. Laos’ air force has only a few dozen aircraft, including about four of the K-8 jets, according to an annual global military survey from the International Institute for Strategic Studies.

Nearby countries such as Vietnam, Thailand and Singapore will likely watch to see if Ban Keun’s runway is lengthened to host bombers or surveillance aircraft. Many Chinese fighter jets and other aircraft can take off from runways shorter than the one at Ban Keun, but standard Chinese air force runways are often notably longer.

Countries in Southeast Asia generally try to stay friendly with Beijing, while many also look to the United States to counterbalance Chinese power. Singapore and Thailand, in particular, provide logistic support for U.S. forces in the region, said Professor Lin. Vietnam, which has had acrimonious boundary disputes with China, has also turned to the United States.

Rear Admiral Surasant Kongsiri, a spokesman for Thailand’s Ministry of Defense, said Laos had the right to decide whether to allow China to operate a base there, Reuters reported. “Nevertheless, Thailand will continue to closely monitor developments,” he said.

Ban Keun has been used by a foreign military before. During the Vietnam War, an airfield there served as a forward base for covert American support operations that were carried out under the name Air America.

Construction on the new base began around October 2025 and proceeded swiftly, satellite images show. By May, much of the runway was visible.
